articles.title: Eleições 2026: David Almeida realiza caminhada em Parintins e promete fortalecer setor primário no estado | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato do Avante ao governo do Amazonas defendeu zoneamento econômico ecológico e a compra da produção rural para merenda escolar no estado em agenda nesta quarta-feira (16).
articles.summary: Candidato do Avante ao governo do Amazonas defendeu zoneamento econômico ecológico e a compra da produção rural para merenda escolar no estado em agenda nesta quarta-feira (16).
articles.body:
Candidato ao governo do Amazonas, David Almeida (Avante) cumpriu agenda em Parintins. — Foto: Jean Beltrão/Rede Amazônica

O candidato ao governo do Amazonas, David Almeida ( Avante ), realizou uma caminhada ao lado de apoiadores no município de Parintins, no fim da tarde desta quarta-feira (16). Durante a agenda, ele apresentou propostas para fortalecer o setor primário no estado.

David Almeida disputa o cargo pela coligação "Pra Cima, Amazonas", formada por Avante, Solidariedade, Partido da Renovação Democrática (PRD), Partido Democrático Trabalhista (PDT), Democracia Cristã (DC) e Agir. O candidato é ex-prefeito de Manaus , cumpriu três mandatos como deputado estadual e assumiu interinamente o Governo do Amazonas em 2017.

O candidato afirmou que, caso eleito, pretende realizar o zoneamento econômico ecológico e vai buscar aproximar o governo dos produtores rurais. David também defendeu a compra da produção rural para a merenda escolar da rede pública de ensino.

"Nós precisamos desenvolver o estado do Amazonas através do setor primário. Só vamos conseguir isso através do zoneamento econômico ecológico, dando segurança para todos os agricultores e, acima de tudo, trazer para próximo dos agricultores, para próximo da produção rural, a própria secretaria, o Idam, fortalecendo as cadeias produtivas, comprando essa produção através da merenda escolar do estado do Amazonas e assim a gente vai fortalecer o setor primário", afirmou.

A agenda do candidato começou com uma caminhada em Maués, seguida de encontro com apoiadores e lideranças, e entrevista à rádio local. Durante a tarde, viajou para Barreirinha, onde também realizou caminhada com apoiadores, concedeu entrevista e participou de encontro com lideranças e apoiadores.

A campanha eleitoral começou no dia 16 de agosto em todo o país. Os candidatos já podem fazer propaganda nas ruas e na internet. Na TV e no rádio, a propaganda começou no dia 28 de agosto. O primeiro turno das eleições será no dia 4 de outubro.

articles.title: Pai de Vorcaro pede revogação da prisão e que Fachin destrave processo no STF | G1
articles.standfirst: Henrique Vorcaro foi preso em maio deste ano sob suspeita de integrar o chamado “núcleo violento” do grupo criminoso associado ao banqueiro preso.
articles.summary: Henrique Vorcaro foi preso em maio deste ano sob suspeita de integrar o chamado “núcleo violento” do grupo criminoso associado ao banqueiro preso.
articles.body:
A defesa de Henrique Vorcaro, pai do ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro, pediu nesta quarta-feira (16) a revogação da prisão. Os advogados afirmam que Henrique está preso há mais de 90 dias e que o Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) não julgou até o momento nenhum recurso contra a prisão.

Henrique Vorcaro foi preso em maio deste ano sob suspeita de integrar o chamado “núcleo violento” do grupo criminoso associado ao banqueiro preso, segundo uma fonte da Polícia Federal.

Em junho, o STF confirmou e manteve a prisão preventiva. A operação mirou os nucleos conhecidos como "A Turma" e "Os Meninos", responsáveis por crimes de intimidação, coerção, obtenção de informações sigilosas e invasões a dispositivos informáticos.

A defesa de Henrique Vorcaro citou ainda a indefinição da sessão do STF que decidiria se o ministro Alexandre de Moraes deveria ser investigado pelo seu suposto envolvimento no caso Master.

Ao assumir a relatoria do caso que discute a possível abertura de investigação contra o ministro Alexandre de Moraes, Edson Fachin, presidente da Corte, também determinou que processos relacionados ao Master e ao caso do INSS fossem encaminhados à Presidência, suspendendo a tramitação enquanto a Corte discute quem deve conduzir essas apurações.

Os advogados afirmam que a sessão não resolveu o dilema sobre qual será o órgão competente e qual será o relator para analisar matérias relacionadas ao caso Master. Um pedido de vista do ministro Flávio Dino suspendeu o julgamento desta terça.

Além disso, a defesa pede que o caso seja analisado pela Segunda Turma do STF.

"Ao propósito, por fim, merece destaque o fato de que ali não se discute nenhuma conduta praticada por pessoa com foro privativo nesta Nenhuma! A matéria diz respeito à tal Turma, que seria arregimentada por Daniel Vorcaro, para fins ilícitos. Nenhum político, nenhum Ministro, nenhuma autoridade, enfim, é mencionada naqueles fatos", afirma a defesa.

Henrique Vorcaro, pai de Daniel Vorcaro é preso em BH. — Foto: Redes sociais

articles.title: Domingos Sávio defende redução dos juros e mais crédito para o agronegócio durante visita a Varginha, MG | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato do PL esteve em cooperativas de crédito e de café, além de se reunir com representantes do Sindicato dos Produtores Rurais de Varginha.
articles.summary: Candidato do PL esteve em cooperativas de crédito e de café, além de se reunir com representantes do Sindicato dos Produtores Rurais de Varginha.
articles.body:
O candidato ao Senado Domingos Sávio (PL) cumpriu agenda nesta quarta-feira (16) em Varginha , no Sul de Minas, onde visitou uma cooperativa de crédito, uma cooperativa de café e se reuniu com representantes do Sindicato dos Produtores Rurais. Durante a passagem pela cidade, ele destacou propostas voltadas ao agronegócio, defendeu a ampliação do crédito rural e criticou as taxas de juros para financiamentos no setor.

Durante a visita a Varginha, Domingos Sávio afirmou que o agronegócio é uma de suas principais bandeiras e lembrou a atuação como produtor rural, presidente de cooperativa e de sindicato rural. O candidato disse que pretende levar essa pauta para o Senado caso seja eleito.

"Olha, essa é a minha origem, eu sou produtor rural, fui presidente de cooperativa, de sindicato rural e como deputado eu sempre defendi o produtor rural. Essa região de Minas é um orgulho para nós, é uma região de grande produção, gerando muito emprego, gerando riqueza. Juros altíssimos, falta de crédito, muitas das vezes o produtor sendo maltratado por um governo que, ao invés de respeitar o produtor, chega a tratá-lo como um criminoso", disse o candidato.

Domingos Sávio defende redução dos juros e mais crédito para o agronegócio durante visita a Varginha — Foto: Reprodução EPTV

Durante a visita, Domingos Sávio também abordou a relação entre produtores rurais e trabalhadores do campo. O candidato afirmou defender um ambiente de diálogo e respeito entre os setores.

"Nós precisamos de harmonia, de paz no campo, de respeito a quem produz alimentos. É isso que eu sempre defendi como deputado e pretendo defender no Senado", disse o candidato.

Além dos compromissos em Varginha, Domingos Sávio esteve na Santa Casa de Nepomuceno e participou de uma caminhada com apoiadores na cidade. Em Três Pontas, o candidato visitou uma cooperativa de café, uma empresa de logística e uma fábrica de brinquedos. Ao final da agenda na região, seguiu para São Lourenço.

articles.title: Moraes vota para igualar licença maternidade de mães biológica e adotivas; julgamento é suspenso | G1
articles.standfirst: Relator também fixou proibição de distinção em razão de vínculo de trabalho. Toffoli, Dino e Cármen Lúcia acompanharam o voto. Julgamento será retomado na próxima semana.
articles.summary: Relator também fixou proibição de distinção em razão de vínculo de trabalho. Toffoli, Dino e Cármen Lúcia acompanharam o voto. Julgamento será retomado na próxima semana.
articles.body:
O ministro do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) Alexandre de Moraes votou nesta quarta-feira (16) para igualar os direitos de mães adotivas e biológicas em relação à licença maternidade.

O ministro, relator da ação apresentada pela Procuradoria Geral da República (PGR), foi acompanhado pelo ministros Dias Toffoli, Cármen Lúcia e Flávio Dino. O julgamento foi suspenso em razão do horário e será retomado na próxima semana.

Pelo voto de Moraes, todas as mães, sejam biológicas ou adotantes, terão direito a licença maternidade de idêntico conteúdo: afastamento remunerado de 120 dias, prorrogável por mais 60 dias.

O prazo é contado a partir do 9º mês de gestação, do parto, da adoção ou da obtenção da guarda para fins de adoção, bem como da alta hospitalar do recém nascido ou da mãe — o que ocorrer primeiro — independentemente da natureza do vínculo laboral ou funcional da beneficiária, seja CLT ou estatutária.

Moraes negou apenas um pedido da PGR, que previa o compartilhamento de licença parental entre os integrantes do núcleo familiar.

Atualmente, mães biológicas que têm vínculo de trabalho estatutário na esfera federal têm 120 dias de licença remunerada. Já as mães adotantes têm 90 dias de licença se a criança tiver até um ano e 30 dias se a criança tiver mais de 1 ano.

“Não há constitucionalidade nem em desfavor da maternidade adotiva nem tampouco uma segunda dicriminação em relação à maternidade adotiva, o período de afastamento vai sendo graduado de acordo com a idade da criança adotada”, afirmou Moraes.

A CLT já equipara mães biológicas e adotantes para fins de licença maternidade, enquanto algumas leis estatutárias ainda mantêm diferenças formais para adotantes.

O STF vem entendendo que essa distinção viola a Constituição e a PGR pede a uniformização definitiva das regras para todas as categorias.

Mãos mãe filho bebê maternidade — Foto: Reprodução/TV Integração

Em 2023, o Supremo decidiu que não é possível discriminar o tempo de licença-maternidade concedida à mãe biológica e à mãe adotante e citou princípios da dignidade humana, da igualdade entre filhos biológicos e adotados, da doutrina da proteção integral e dos princípios da prioridade e do melhor interesse da criança.

No entanto, a PGR sustenta que a decisão serviu de base apenas para órgãos do Poder Judiciário e não alcançou a administração pública . Por isso, a decisão não suspendeu a eficácia das leis em contrário e a discriminação continuou ocorrendo.

A ação pede a declaração de incompatibilidade das normas com a Constituição para, com isso, vincular tanto órgãos do Poder Judiciário, quanto a administração pública.

“Entende-se, portanto, ser cabível esta ação direta, que se dirige não somente a afastar a aplicação de disposições normativas que, na atualidade, acabam por configurar um tratamento discriminatório quanto à concessão de licença parental, como também fixar no plano jurídico-objetivo a tese de que o sistema de proteção parental, há de se submeter a um regime jurídico uniforme, independentemente do vínculo laboral da categoria que dele se beneficie”, argumenta a PGR.

Moraes afirmou que a licença maternidade não é um direito só relacionado à mulher, mas um direito relacionado aos filhos.

“A Constituição protege essas duas pessoas”, disse em seu voto.

“Se todos são filhos, a mãe é mãe de todos, dos filhos naturais, biológicos, adotivos, então a licença maternidade deve ser igual para todos”, afirmou o ministro.

Moraes destacou que os dispositivos contestados estão não só em confronto com os preceitos constitucionais, como com os precedentes do STF.

A ministra Cármen Lúcia destacou que a interpretação trazida pelo relator é mais coerente com a Constituição.

“Mãe é só uma e todo filho é único para nós. O filho é filho e pronto e essa desigualação poderia se constituir da pessoa se sentir distinta também, quando a pessoa contasse pra ela e tudo mais”.

articles.title: 'De dia mostra a bandeira nacional e de noite vai ficar de quatro para os EUA', diz Lula sobre Eduardo e Flávio Bolsonaro | G1
articles.standfirst: Lula afirmou que Flávio Bolsonaro enviou o irmão aos EUA para “tramar contra o Brasil” e voltou a associar a família Bolsonaro a articulações junto ao governo de Donald Trump.
articles.summary: Lula afirmou que Flávio Bolsonaro enviou o irmão aos EUA para “tramar contra o Brasil” e voltou a associar a família Bolsonaro a articulações junto ao governo de Donald Trump.
articles.body:
O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) criticou nesta quarta-feira (16) o candidato à Presidência da República Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) e afirmou que o senador enviou o irmão, deputado cassado Eduardo Bolsonaro, para os Estados Unidos "para tramar contra o Brasil".

"Esse mesmo cidadão do outro lado, ele mandou o irmão dele para os Estados Unidos para tramar contra o Brasil. Está lá o Eduardo Bolsonaro, o traidor da pátria, falando mal do Brasil, pedindo para que o Trump venha fazer intervenção nesse país".

"Esse país não comporta político vira-lata. Esse país não comporta político que de dia mostra a bandeira nacional e de noite vai ficar de quatro para os Estados Unidos, para a bandeira americana. Esse país não comporta isso, porque o Brasil está cansado, o Brasil não quer ser colônia de ninguém. O Brasil quer ser soberano e dirigido por brasileiros e construir o futuro com o suor e o sangue dos brasileiros".

A fala foi durante ato de campanha à reeleição em Brasília (DF).

O presidente tem atribuído a integrantes da família Bolsonaro iniciativas em defesa de medidas adotadas pelo governo do presidente americano, Donald Trump , contra o Brasil e acusa o grupo de tentar pressionar autoridades brasileiras a partir de articulações no exterior.

Eduardo Bolsonaro está nos Estados Unidos e tem mantido contatos com políticos e representantes ligados ao governo americano.

No último ano, Lula passou a associar a atuação do filho do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro às tensões entre Brasil e Estados Unidos e se refere aos filhos do ex-presidente como "traidores da pátria" .

O presidente afirmou ainda que neste final de semana vai aos Estados Unidos participar da Assembleia Geral da Organização das Nações Unidas (ONU) e que vai conversar com o presidente norte-americano, Donald Trump.

"Vou para a reunião da ONU para ter um bate-papo com o Trump e dizer para o Trump não se meta nas eleições do Brasil, o Brasil só tem um dono e o dono do Brasil é o povo brasileiro".

articles.title: Em resposta aos EUA, governo brasileiro nega falhas no combate ao crime organizado  | G1
articles.standfirst: Donald Trump acusou o Brasil de ter falhado no combate às facções criminosas Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) e Comando Vermelho (CV).
articles.summary: Donald Trump acusou o Brasil de ter falhado no combate às facções criminosas Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) e Comando Vermelho (CV).
articles.body:
Em resposta a alegações dos Estados Unidos, o governo brasileiro negou nesta quinta-feira (16) que existam falhas ou omissões no enfrentamento ao crime organizado transnacional.

"A alusão registrada no texto não corresponde à categoria jurídica de descumprimento formal prevista na legislação norte-americana que rege esse mecanismo anual. Trata-se, portanto, de manifestação circunstancial inserida na parte narrativa do documento, sem respaldo em sua parte dispositiva", afirma o governo brasileiro.

No relatório enviado ao Congresso dos EUA na terça-feira (15), o presidente pede que o governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) adote, "com urgência, medidas enérgicas para enfrentar" os grupos. PCC e CV foram incluídos recentemente pelos EUA na lista de organizações terroristas.

As afirmações estão em um documento divulgado pelo Departamento de Estado nesta quarta-feira (16).

O documento diz ainda que, enquanto outros governos do Hemisfério Ocidental estão tomando "medidas corajosas" para erradicar cartéis, o Brasil não está enfrentando o PCC e o CV.

"Essas organizações terroristas brasileiras representam uma ameaça crescente à paz e à segurança em todo o mundo, e o governo brasileiro precisa urgentemente adotar medidas firmes para enfrentá-las e derrotá-las antes que se espalhem e cresçam", diz presidente norte-americano.

Em nota, o ministério da Justiça afirma que as alegações do governo americano desconsideram medidas adotadas pelo governo brasileiro, como a Lei Antifacção, aprovada pelo Congresso Nacional e sancionada por Lula e a cooperação já existente entre Brasil e EUA no combate ao crime organizado transnacional.

"Também não levaria em consideração as dezenas de milhares de operações de combate ao crime, por forças federais, com bilhões de reais de prejuízo aos criminosos, bem como as múltiplas ações implementadas em 2026 no âmbito do Programa Brasil contra o Crime Organizado, lançado em maio último, que sufoca economicamente as facções, fortalece o sistema prisional, qualifica a investigação de homicídios e enfrenta o tráfico de armas".

Além disso, afirma que o combate ao crime organizado é prioridade do governo federal e "vem sendo conduzido de forma permanente por meio de ações de inteligência, investigação, integração entre as forças de segurança e cooperação internacional e jurídica".

Presos fazem rebelião na Penitenciária de Junqueirópolis, em São Paulo, em 14 de maio de 2006. O motim começou às 7 da manhã, quando familiares entravam para a visita. Os rebelados subiram no telhado e prenderam faixas na caixa d´água com os dizeres: 'PCC, paz, justiça e liberdade' e 'Contra a Opressão' — Foto: Alex Silva/Estadão Conteúdo/Arquivo

Leia a íntegra da nota do governo brasileiro:

Em 15 de setembro, o governo dos Estados Unidos enviou ao seu Congresso lista anual dos países que identifica como maiores produtores e de trânsito de drogas. O Brasil não integra a lista de 23 países citados.

Entretanto, foi objeto de críticas laterais no documento. O governo brasileiro refuta quaisquer alegações de que existam falhas ou omissões no enfrentamento ao crime organizado transnacional.

A posição estampada na referida nota desconsideraria, se acolhida em todos os seus termos, os esforços do Governo Federal no enfrentamento ao crime organizado, como a Lei Antifacção, sancionada em março de 2026, que prevê penas mais severas para líderes de facções e cria mecanismos que asfixiam suas operações.

Também não levaria em consideração as dezenas de milhares de operações de combate ao crime, por forças federais, com bilhões de reais de prejuízo aos criminosos, bem como as múltiplas ações implementadas em 2026 no âmbito do Programa Brasil contra o Crime Organizado, lançado em maio último, que sufoca economicamente as facções, fortalece o sistema prisional, qualifica a investigação de homicídios e enfrenta o tráfico de armas.

A manifestação norte-americana desconsideraria a robusta cooperação já existente entre Brasil e EUA no combate ao crime organizado transnacional. Além disso, convém frisar a proposta entregue pessoalmente pelo presidente Lula no dia 7/5/2026, em Washington, com detalhamento de medidas conjuntas de enfrentamento à lavagem de dinheiro, compartilhamento de inteligência e combate ao tráfico de armas. Até o momento, permanecemos no aguardo da possível resposta do governo dos EUA.

O Brasil não foi incluído na relação de países formalmente classificados pelos EUA como principais rotas de trânsito ou de produção ilícita de drogas. A alusão registrada no texto não corresponde à categoria jurídica de descumprimento formal prevista na legislação norte-americana que rege esse mecanismo anual. Trata-se, portanto, de manifestação circunstancial inserida na parte narrativa do documento, sem respaldo em sua parte dispositiva.

O Ministério da Justiça e Segurança Pública (MJSP) reafirma que o combate ao crime organizado é prioridade do Governo Federal e vem sendo conduzido de forma permanente por meio de ações de inteligência, investigação, integração entre as forças de segurança e cooperação internacional e jurídica.

O Governo brasileiro seguirá atuando de forma soberana e coordenada no enfrentamento às organizações criminosas, como demonstram os resultados obtidos nos últimos anos. O enfrentamento ao crime organizado transnacional exige atuação contínua, integração entre instituições e cooperação. Essa é a estratégia adotada pelo Estado brasileiro e que continuará sendo fortalecida em defesa da segurança da população brasileira.

articles.summary: Confira as atividades de campanha de ACM Neto; Jerônimo Rodrigues; Aroldo Felix; Maria Bona; Ariel Capistrano; e Ronaldo Mansur.
articles.body:
Candidatos ao governo da Bahia em 2026 — Foto: Reprodução/DivulgaCand

Os candidatos ao governo da Bahia cumpriram compromissos de campanha nesta quarta-feira (16). Entre as atividades do dia, estiveram entrevistas, caminhadas, carreatas, panfletagem e reuniões, em Salvador e cidades da região metropolitana.

O candidato do União Brasil foi entrevistado pela manhã em uma emissora de rádio, em Salvador. Depois, ao lado de integrantes da chapa, percorreu as ruas do bairro do Engenho Velho de Brotas, também na capital baiana.

Em seguida, se reuniu com lideranças políticas de municípios baianos. Pela noite, participou de uma caminhada em Castro Alves.

O candidato à reeleição pelo PT participou de carreatas durante a tarde nos municípios de Madre de Deus e Candeias.

O candidato da Unidade Popular fez panfletagem pela manhã no bairro do Uruguai, em Salvador. À tarde, participou do lançamento do Comitê em Defesa da Soberania Nacional e da Universidade Pública, no campus da Universidade do Estado da Bahia (Uneb).

A candidata do Partido da Causa Operária não divulgou a agenda de campanha.

O candidato do Democracia Cristã se reuniu pela manhã com a coordenação de campanha, em Salvador. À tarde, visitou o município de Simões Filho.

O candidato do PSOL participou pela manhã de uma entrevista ao vivo no telejornal da Bahia Meio Dia, na sede da Rede Bahia, em Salvador. Depois, participou de uma reunião com lideranças do movimento sem-teto, em Lauro de Freitas.

articles.title: Eleições 2026: Omar Aziz participa de entrevista em Manaus e promete reduzir fila do SisReg | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato do PSD ao governo do Amazonas apresentou propostas para a saúde pública no estado.
articles.summary: Candidato do PSD ao governo do Amazonas apresentou propostas para a saúde pública no estado.
articles.body:
Candidato ao governo do Amazonas, Omar Aziz (PSD) cumpriu agenda no Centro de Manaus. — Foto: Rede Amazônica

O candidato ao governo do Amazonas, Omar Aziz ( PSD ), cumpriu agenda no Largo São Sebastião, no Centro de Manaus , nesta quarta-feira (16). Durante o compromisso, participou de uma entrevista a uma emissora de televisão, conversou com eleitores e apresentou propostas para a saúde.

Omar Aziz disputa o cargo pela coligação "Força Amazonas", formada pelo Partido Social Democrático (PSD), Movimento Democrático Brasileiro (MDB) e Republicanos. O candidato já foi governador do estado entre 2010 e 2014 e, posteriormente, foi eleito senador e reeleito ao cargo em 2022.

Durante a agenda, Omar falou que pretende reduzir a fila do Sisreg no sistema público de saúde do estado. Também prometeu ampliar os atendimentos para consultas e exames através da valorização e contratação de novos profissionais de saúde.

"Através de contratação de clinicas particulares, hospitais particulares, laboratórios particulares, tanto de imagem como laboratoriais, porque hoje essa fila esta estrangulada e muitas pessoas estão morrendo na fila do SisReg. Além de ampliar a rede de atendimento estadual, a gente vai ter que fazer isso nos 100 primeiros dias para que a gente reduza e acabe definitivamente com a fila do SisReg", afirmou.

A agenda do candidato continuou pela tarde com uma reunião com lideranças do interior do Amazonas. À noite, participou de evento popular com apoiadores em Manaus.

A campanha eleitoral começou no dia 16 de agosto em todo o país. Os candidatos já podem fazer propaganda nas ruas e na internet. Na TV e no rádio, a propaganda começou no dia 28 de agosto. O primeiro turno das eleições será no dia 4 de outubro.

articles.title: Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann’s wife files defamation case against Majithia, Harsimrat and Khaira
articles.summary: CM Bhagwant Mann’s wife Gurpreet Kaur files criminal defamation case in Chandigarh against Majithia, Harsimrat Badal and Khaira over allegations.
articles.body: CHANDIGARH: Gurpreet Kaur, wife of Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann, on Wednesday filed a criminal defamation complaint in a Chandigarh district court against SAD functionaries Bikram Singh Majithia and Harsimrat Kaur Badal and Sukhpal Singh Khaira of Congress for allegedly levelling false allegations against her.The complaint was filed under Sections 210 and 222 of BNSS for offences under Section 356 of BNS and seeks to summon and prosecute the three.Gurpreet Kaur claimed the allegations portrayed her as seeking money to influence the govt machinery to help a rape accused. articles.body:
President Trump will stump for GOP Senate nominee Michael Whatley in North Carolina on Wednesday evening, seeking to rally support for the former Republican National Committee chair.

Whatley is running against former Gov. Roy Cooper (D) for the seat currently held by Sen. Thom Tillis (R), who will retire at the end of the term. The event marks Trump’s first campaign stop since last week’s GOP midterm convention , as Republicans fight to maintain their control of Congress next year.

Recent polling shows Cooper leading Whatley by double digits — 49 percent to 38 percent — among likely voters in the Tar Heel State. While the president won North Carolina in his three presidential elections, the same Elon poll found more than half of respondents disapprove of his job performance as affordability ranks high for voters in the state.

The campaign event in Gastonia, N.C., is scheduled to begin at 7 p.m. EDT.

articles.title: Trump’s latest branding battle: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: In today’s edition, Andrea Mitchell dives into the latest in the Kennedy Center saga. Plus, we examine new Republican defectors on the House’s Iran war vote.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Andrea Mitchell dives into the latest in the Kennedy Center saga. Plus, we examine new Republican defectors on the House’s Iran war vote. — Adam Wollner What’s in a name? At the Kennedy Center, a multimillion-dollar fight Analysis by Andrea Mitchell As a private businessman, Donald Trump became known as an expert at branding — specifically, by putting his name on everything from buildings to steaks. His hugely expanded power as president has given him even more opportunities: an airport, the U.S. Institute for Peace, savings accounts for children and U.S. currency, to name a few. Now, his branding efforts are at the center of a fierce legal battle over a hallowed memorial to a slain president. During a pivotal meeting of the new Trump-dominated Kennedy Center board yesterday, Trump got into a shouting match with Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, a holdover ex officio member of the board. According to multiple people listening to the virtual meeting who described it to NBC News, Trump called Beatty incompetent and destructive, while she called him unprofessional. The board ultimately voted to close the center for renovations. Trump has erupted online with angry posts several times over recent months since a federal court issued a preliminary injunction for now that rejects his bid to add his name to the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts’ marble facade. The White House obeyed the order to take the name down but covered the altered signage with a tarp so it cannot be seen. The symbolism has legal significance. Unlike other monuments and buildings Trump has changed in the past year and a half, the Kennedy Center was created by an act of Congress in 1964 as the sole memorial to the assassinated president in the nation’s capital. As such, it is comparable to the Lincoln and Jefferson memorials. Opponents argue the name can be changed only by an act of Congress, not by a presidential executive order. Trump’s handpicked board replaced the former board and named Trump as chairman. Trump fired the former chairman, private equity billionaire and philanthropist David Rubenstein, who had donated $120 million of his own money to the arts center. Critics say Trump’s takeover cratered the center’s programming, costing it millions in ticket sales. The White House argues that the programming was “woke” and that the center was dilapidated and had been poorly run for years. Both sides agree the center needs renovations, but the former board members argue that has been done in the past without closing the entire building. While lawyers fight it out, Trump pledged $17 million of his own money toward the renovations — but only if his name is added back to the facade. In a Truth Social post calling for an expedited appeal, Trump wrote, “If the ruling is a negative one, which it should not be, and is not overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court, the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place.” Typically, the center hosted as many as 3,000 performances a year. Threatened with closure, the Washington Opera moved in January to a nearby university stage. The National Symphony Orchestra, the center’s principal tenant since 1971, delayed choosing other venues for months while the legal slugfest continued. Finally, in August, after having lost season subscriptions and needing revenue, the NSO found six smaller concert halls in Washington, Virginia and Maryland for the coming season. Dance and jazz programming has been canceled. And the board has announced that signature events, including the annual Kennedy Center Honors and the Mark Twain Prize, will be held in alternative locations. Owen Hayes contributed. New GOP cracks emerge over the Iran war as midterms loom By Adam Wollner For the third time, the GOP-led House last night approved a war powers resolution that would prohibit President Donald Trump from taking further military action in Iran without congressional approval. And this time, three new Republicans voted for it: Rep. Nancy Mace of South Carolina and Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn of Iowa. After she lost her primary for governor, Mace is on her way out of Congress. But Miller-Meeks and Nunn are running for re-election in battleground districts with control of the House up for grabs. The Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates both their races as “toss ups.”Miller-Meeks, who served in the Army for 24 years, and Nunn, a colonel in the Air Force Reserve, both said they wouldn’t support an “open-ended war.” “The President needs to present a plan to Congress and the American people for how this ends so we can focus on bringing our soldiers home and lowering prices,” Miller-Meeks said on X. Nunn noted that two service members from Iowa have died as a result of the war. “Congress owes them, their families, and every American in uniform clear objectives and constitutional oversight,” Nunn wrote. “With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization.” Notably, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth campaigned with Nunn in Iowa last month. The war powers resolution is nonbinding, meaning it’s largely symbolic. But seven House Republicans’ now supporting the measure underscores the political pressure the party is under with the midterms quickly approaching. A national Marquette University Law School poll found that 26% of adults approve of Trump’s handling of the Iran war, a new low in the survey, while Democrats opened up an 8-point lead on the generic congressional ballot among registered voters. Eyeing the exit: Last night’s vote appears it will be the last one on the Iran war before the midterms. The House is set to leave Washington tonight until Nov. 9 after GOP leaders said they were canceling votes set for tomorrow, Scott Wong and Kyle Stewart report. (The Senate will remain in session for the next three weeks.) The change in schedule means the House won’t vote on a resolution from Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky. — a lead proponent of the war powers measures — to impeach Hegseth until after Election Day. Hegseth had campaigned this year for Massie’s primary opponent, former Navy SEAL Ed Gallrein. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said, “It’s time for our members to go home to their districts and make their case to the American people, to go and explain all the great things we’ve done.” That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner and Lauren Zola. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

articles.title: Kiley says he won’t caucus with GOP next year if reelected
articles.summary: Independent Rep. Kevin Kiley (Calif.), a former Republican, said he will not caucus with Republicans next year if he wins reelection. “Congressman Kiley, much has been made about your decision to switch from Republican to independent next year. Are you still going to caucus with Republicans?” Semafor’s Nicholas Wu asked the California representative at a…
articles.body:
Independent Rep. Kevin Kiley (Calif.), a former Republican, said he will not caucus with Republicans next year if he wins reelection.

“Congressman Kiley, much has been made about your decision to switch from Republican to independent next year. Are you still going to caucus with Republicans?” Semafor’s Nicholas Wu asked the California representative at a Wednesday event for the outlet.

“No. I’m working on changing the rules of the House to get rid of this crazy policy where you have to be formally affiliated with one caucus or the other simply to get committee seats,” Kiley responded.

“And so, I’m an independent member now, and yet the rules of the House force me to say, ‘Okay, as a formality, for the purposes of committee assignments, I’m going to conference with one side or the other,’” he added.

Kiley is currently caucusing with the House Republicans, but in March he announced that he would formally leave the GOP to become an independent.

The Golden State lawmaker had announced a few days prior that he would make a midterm reelection bid as an independent, but he accelerated the process shortly after, saying he was going to file a letter with the House clerk immediately to change his party identification.

“I will be the sole independent member of the House of Representatives,” Kiley told reporters in a virtual press conference at the time. “We’re going to be submitting the letter to the clerk today.”

Kiley has said his decision to leave the GOP was based in his disgust with the gerrymandering battle that’s raging around the country, with legislators in red and blue states racing to redraw their maps for partisan advantage in the midterms.

Kiley is set for a showdown in November against Democratic challenger Richard Pan for California’s 6th Congressional District.

He faces a risky race, with nonpartisan handicapper Cook Political Report placing his race in the solidly Democratic column.

articles.title: Fox News Poll: Squeezed by costs, frustrated voters turn to the Democrats
articles.summary: Trump's 39% job approval and a 26-point endorsement gap could spell trouble for GOP candidates, a new Fox News survey finds before Election Day.
articles.body: Roughly three-quarters of voters have rated economic conditions negatively for the past year, and more than three times as many say they are falling behind financially as getting ahead, according to a Fox News survey released Wednesday. And by a wide margin, the Democrats are considered the party that would better handle inflation at a time when the cost of living and the economy are voters’ top concerns. Costs of everyday items are a hardship for voters: 61% say gas prices are a major problem, up from 48% two years ago, while 52% say the same for healthcare costs, up from 44%. Majorities also view housing costs (54%, down from 60%) and grocery prices (62%, down from 66%) as major problems. FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS OPPOSE THE IRAN WAR, SEE PROLONGED COMMITMENT Views on tariffs have grown more negative since last summer, with a high of 64% saying tariffs hurt the U.S. economy, up from 57%. Most Democrats and independents say tariffs hurt, while views among Republicans are mixed (41% help, 36% hurt, 21% no difference). FOX NEWS POLL: COOL YOUR SERVERS! VOTERS REJECT DATA CENTERS Overall, nearly two-thirds of voters (63%) say the Trump administration has made the economy worse, including a quarter of Republicans. All of this contributes to greater pessimism about the future. The portion saying life will be worse for the next generation has risen from 53% two years ago to 62% last year and 68% today, just two points below the high of 70% in 2022. Only 8% are enthusiastic about how the government is working, with another 23% satisfied. A 68% majority is unhappy, including a high of 33% who are "angry" — driven by 56% of Democrats and 36% of independents vs. just 9% of Republicans. Despite these economic headwinds and with 48 days until Election Day, maybe the good news for the Republicans is that the Democrats' advantage on the congressional ballot has stayed in the single digits. If the election were today, 51% say they would back the Democratic candidate in their House district and 44% the Republican. The Democrats’ 7-point edge is just outside the survey’s margin of sampling error. Since January, the Democrats have been preferred by 5-7 points. Women, those under age 35, Hispanic voters and Whites with a college degree give Democrats their edge, while White men and non-college Whites are strengths for the GOP. Party loyalty slightly favors the Democrats, as more of them (97%) than Republicans (92%) support their party’s candidate. Independents favor the Democratic candidate 53-31%, with 14% undecided. Higher engagement boosts Democrats: 64% are extremely interested in the election compared to 53% of Republicans (+11 D margin). And more Democrats (71%) than Republicans (65%) rate their likelihood of voting as a 10 on a 10-point scale, meaning they feel certain they will vote (+6 D margin). Among those certain to vote, the Democrats’ lead in the generic ballot grew to 11 points (54-43%). The edge holds among those in "close" counties, where the 2024 presidential vote between President Trump and former Vice President Harris was within 10 points; the Democratic candidate is favored by 9 points, 52-43%. "When pundits and analysts talk about the fundamentals favoring the Democrats in this midterm, they are mostly referring to the economy," says Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who conducts the Fox News Poll with Democratic pollster Chris Anderson. "Time is running out for the administration and its supporters to convince voters that things are improving." Those with a negative view of both the Democratic and the Republican Party ("double haters") favor the Democratic candidate in their district by a 26-point margin. Voters trust Democrats on most issues in the survey: inflation (by 15 points), large AI data centers (+14), corruption (+11), and foreign policy (+10). The parties are about evenly rated on immigration (R +1). Prior to this summer, the Republicans held a four-year advantage on immigration, and they led on foreign policy until January of this year. Four years ago, Republicans were preferred by 9 points on inflation. Democrats have improved their ratings on inflation by 5 points just since July. Voters trusting Democrats on inflation are more likely to attribute this to Republican failures (51%) than confidence that Democratic policies are likely to reduce prices (47%). Those views contribute to Trump’s 39% job approval (61% disapprove). His approval has not exceeded 39% since April, when it stood at 42%. His current rating trails former President Biden’s 43% at this point in 2022 and aligns with former President Obama’s 38% before the 2014 midterms. Trump received 43% approval on immigration, 37% on foreign policy (one point above his record low), and 24% on inflation (matching a previous low). Trump’s standing puts him in a difficult spot to help GOP candidates this year. He lags his party in popularity, holding a 24-point net negative favorability rating (38-62%), unchanged since July. Sixty percent of voters think the U.S. made the wrong decision in taking military action against Iran, and 77% of that group favor the Democratic candidate in their district. Four years ago, more voters said a Trump endorsement made them less likely to support a candidate by a 15-point margin. Today, that’s a 26-point gap (25% more likely, 51% less likely). Still, Trump’s approval matters within the GOP: 52% of Republicans and 75% of MAGA Republicans say it increases their support. In addition, 53% say the Trump administration is more corrupt than previous administrations compared to 26% who say it is less corrupt. Both major parties are viewed negatively: the Democratic Party is underwater by 11 points (44% favorable, 55% unfavorable) and the Republican Party by 17 (41-58%). Nearly two-thirds support raising taxes on the wealthy to expand government programs (65%) and redistribute wealth (63%). However, 52% disagree with increasing taxes on the wealthy so that "nobody gets too rich." Still, dissatisfaction with capitalism has grown. Fifty-seven percent say the way capitalism works in the U.S. these days doesn’t give people a fair shot, up from 42% in 2019. That shift spans political views, increasing among Democrats (by 17 points), Republicans (+13), and independents (+22). Poll-pourri When asked what the most important issue is facing the country unprompted by a list, 34% of voters say the cost of living and 14% say the economy/jobs. The next closest are immigration (8%) and Republicans/Trump/MAGA (7%). Only a handful mention issues like the war with Iran (4%), corruption (4%), healthcare (4%), or AI/data centers (1%). MAGA holds a 5-point favorability edge compared with the Democratic Socialists of America (35% vs. 30%), although 15% are unable to rate the DSA. Nearly 3 in 10 Democrats view the DSA negatively, and 3 in 10 Republicans view MAGA negatively. Overall, 59% view labor unions favorably, including 48% of Republicans and 73% of Democrats. Eighty-one percent of voters favor banning Congress members and their immediate family and staff from trading stocks (up from 75% in January), including 8 in 10 Democrats, Republicans, and independents. CLICK HERE FOR CROSSTABS AND TOPLINE Conducted September 11-14, 2026, under the direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News survey includes interviews with a sample of 1,211 registered voters randomly selected from a national voter file. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (96) and cellphones (821) or completed the survey online after receiving a text (294). Results based on the full sample have a margin of sampling error of ±3 percentage points. Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling error, question wording and order can influence results. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education and area variables to ensure the demographics are representative of the registered voter population. Sources for developing weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis, and voter file data. Fox News’ Victoria Balara contributed to this report.

articles.title: Democrats embraced AI’s growth before Trump came along; now, they want to slow it down
articles.summary: Barack Obama is urging Washington to slow AI development. But, in 2016, his White House praised the technology as the cutting edge of innovation.
articles.body: Some of the Democratic Party’s most prominent voices are pushing for tighter limits on artificial intelligence, including former President Barack Obama, who has joined calls for a slower pace of frontier AI development after years of Democratic leaders touting the technology’s economic and strategic potential. "We need government — and specifically our leaders in Washington — to get proactive in coming up with concrete proposals, laws and regulations that deal with serious safety concerns, anticipate AI’s impact on jobs and our kids and make sure that AI’s benefits are widely spread," Obama said in a statement Monday night. Obama’s latest comments put greater emphasis on slowing frontier AI development than his White House did in 2016, when his administration highlighted the technology’s economic potential while also warning about disruption and calling for policy responses. AI EXTINCTION WARNINGS DOMINATE HEADLINES AFTER EX-ANTHROPIC EMPLOYEE'S VIRAL POST Democrats have long paired enthusiasm for AI’s economic and strategic potential with warnings about its risks, but some of the party’s most prominent voices are now going further, calling for a slower pace of frontier AI development and tougher limits on how the technology is built and deployed. Attorney General Todd Blanche argued Tuesday that Democrats’ renewed focus on the potential risks of artificial intelligence should not be treated as "breaking news," suggesting the timing, months before the midterm elections, is politically significant. "Every Democrat senator suddenly races to a microphone to talk about AI after being eerily silent for months and months, a month. So, to talk about the timing of this as being nothing but an effort to influence the midterms, I shouldn't have to say that out loud, of course," said Blanche. The comments came as President Donald Trump has made rapid AI development and the data centers needed to power it a priority, while the administration promotes the technology’s potential economic benefits and faces growing political scrutiny over the cost and impact of expanding data-center infrastructure. Obama issued a statement Monday on X, writing that AI is "moving at lightning speed – and even faster than those who are engineering it can keep up with." "Given what we know about technology, we can’t stuff AI back in a box. But we can collectively determine how it's developed and how it’s used, rather than sitting back and letting AI and its fallout happen to us," he wrote. He called for regulation, saying choices to slow down should not be left up to the tech companies. Any "potential catastrophe will depend on the choices that we make right now," said Obama. ANTHROPIC CEO CALLS ON AI INDUSTRY TO SLOW DOWN TECH RACE, DRAWING SUPPORT FROM ELON MUSK, SAM ALTMAN In 2016, Obama’s White House touted AI’s potential to open new markets and drive progress across industries while warning about job disruption and broader safety and policy challenges. "Advances in AI technology hold incredible potential to help the United States stay on the cutting edge of innovation," the White House said in its December 2016 Artificial Intelligence, Automation, and the Economy report. "Advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology and related fields have opened up new markets and new opportunities for progress in critical areas such as health, education, energy, economic inclusion, social welfare, and the environment. … AI should be welcomed for its potential economic benefits," the report added. Similarly, then-Vice President Kamala Harris said in January 2025 that "it is imperative that the United States remain the global leader on AI" as the Biden administration moved to speed up the buildout needed to support large-scale AI operations. The Biden administration announced an executive order aimed at accelerating AI infrastructure in the U.S., including large data centers and clean-energy projects, as the administration sought to keep the country ahead of its global competitors. Harris has also recently called for slowing the pace of frontier AI development, arguing that the technology is advancing at an "alarming speed" and urging Congress to establish stronger oversight and safety standards. "The frontier of artificial intelligence is advancing at an alarming speed. Over the weekend, industry leaders voiced support for an idea that the American people and many AI researchers in their own labs have been calling for: We must responsibly slow the pace of frontier AI development," she wrote. SEVEN-FIGURE BLITZ AS GOP EMBRACES PUSH TO COMPETE WITH CHINA IN BOOMING NEW TECH SPACE AI and data centers have quickly become a major midterm issue, as concerns over electricity costs, jobs and the rapid buildout draw increasing attention from candidates in both parties. Fox News Digital reached out to Obama, Harris and Schumer's teams for comment.

articles.title: Kamala Harris to campaign with Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan
articles.summary: The former vice president endorsed El-Sayed after he won the Senate Democratic primary in Michigan, where Trump beat her by less than 2 percentage points in 2024.
articles.body: Former Vice President Kamala Harris will campaign with Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan next week, a spokesperson for Harris confirmed to NBC News on Wednesday. El-Sayed, a former public health official, faces one of the most competitive Senate races in the country this year against former Rep. Mike Rogers. “Vice President Harris looks forward to returning to Michigan to help turn out the vote in this critical state. While there, she will highlight the issue of Black maternal health, joined by Dr. El-Sayed,” Harris spokesperson Eduardo Negrón said in a statement. “It is critical we flip the Senate so we can bring down prices and stand up to Donald Trump’s corruption.” Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., is retiring, and Democrats are seeking to hold on to his seat and potentially gain a Senate majority by flipping Republican-held seats in other states. Meanwhile, Republicans face headwinds like inflation and an unpopular war in Iran as they aim to maintain or expand their control of the Senate. Harris, who lost to Donald Trump in the 2024 election, endorsed El-Sayed in August after he won a competitive primary against Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens. Roxie Richner, a spokesperson for El-Sayed, told NBC News on Wednesday that “Abdul is thrilled to welcome Vice President Harris to Michigan for a conversation about improving Black maternal health and bringing down healthcare costs.” Richner added: “He looks forward to hearing directly from Black women and healthcare providers and discussing how he’ll continue that work in the Senate. There’s no better choice for Michiganders than Abdul when it comes to making healthcare more affordable, and he’s grateful Vice President Harris will join him in spreading that message.” Michigan has been a competitive battleground state in statewide and national elections for years. In 2028, it will be the fifth state to vote in the Democratic nominating contest for the presidential election. Harris has decided to campaign there amid speculation that she may run for president again in two years. In 2024, Trump beat Harris in Michigan by less than 2 percentage points on his way back to the White House. The same year, Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., beat Rogers in a Senate race by less than 1 point. Negrón added that while she is in Michigan, Harris will also meet with local elected officials and faith-based leaders. The race between El-Sayed and Rogers has gotten increasingly nasty in recent weeks. El-Sayed has targeted Rogers for accepting corporate donations, repeatedly accusing him of representing corporate interests. Alongside a video highlighting Rogers’ acceptance of campaign donations from pharmaceutical companies, El-Sayed wrote on X that Michiganders “are *literally* sick of Mike Rogers’ corruption.” In another post accusing Rogers of pushing to raise the retirement age nationally, El-Sayed wrote, “He’s a corrupt coward who cares only about his and his donors’ profits and nothing about people.” On the other side of the aisle, Vice President JD Vance has called El-Sayed “evil,” telling people at an event in Michigan last month, “I realize that there’s something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil and on the rise in the United States of America today.” El-Sayed has faced backlash for having accepted support from and campaigned with Twitch streamer Hasan Piker during the Democratic primary campaign. Republicans have sought to tie Piker’s past controversial comments about the 9/11 terrorist attacks to El-Sayed, who has disavowed them. Piker has also apologized for the remarks. El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim U.S. senator, has accused Republicans of Islamophobic attacks against him. Shortly after his primary victory, the National Republican Senatorial Committee posted a video on X calling him “radical” and “dangerous,” using his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed. In an interview last month with NBC News’ “Meet the Press,” El-Sayed called the attacks similar to ones levied against former President Barack Obama, whose full name is Barack Hussein Obama. “We always knew they were going to go here. I mean, notice how they chose to use my full name in echoes to exactly what they did against President Obama,” El-Sayed said at the time. “At the end of the day, it’s not radical to believe that people should be able to afford their groceries,” he added. “It’s not radical to believe that you should have healthcare in this country.”

articles.title: Democrats begrudgingly hand Trump victory on tariffs in sprawling sanctions bill
articles.summary: Several Democrats joined Republicans to pass the Russia sanctions bill, but critics warn Trump could use broad tariff authority against allies.
articles.body: Several Democrats voted with Republicans to pass a sweeping sanctions package targeting Russia Wednesday, handing President Donald Trump a key authority the left has long raged against. The House of Representatives passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, named after the late Republican senator who was one of Ukraine's biggest champions in Congress until his sudden death in July. The legislation passed in a 262 to 159 vote. Fifty-three Democrats voted with 203 Republicans to pass the bill. Seven Republicans and 152 Democrats opposed it. It comes despite opposition from key Democrats over a provision giving Trump tariff authority over countries fueling Russia's war in Ukraine. HOUSE DEMS FACE TRUMP TARIFF DILEMMA AS MAJOR RUSSIA SANCTIONS BILL HEADS TO FLOOR "What we're not for is giving more tariff authority to this president," Rep. Richard Neal, D-Mass., said during debate on the bill. "There is no guarantee in this legislation that the president could not use these tariffs against Ukraine if he decided to do so. There is no guarantee in this legislation that the president can impose these tariffs on Russia, with the enthusiasm that our friends on the other side have offered." House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said, "The manner in which this bill has been written doesn't require the president of the United States to impose sanctions on Russia. In fact, there are so many loopholes written into the bill, I believe that it's very unlikely that the sanctions relief contemplated in the legislation will ever see the light of day." LINDSEY GRAHAM'S FINAL MISSION TO PUNISH PUTIN CLEARS SENATE AFTER YEARLONG FIGHT The bill was led in the House by Rep. Michael McCaul, R-Texas, a longtime supporter of Ukraine. "This is a critical time in history, a time my friend Lindsey Graham described as a magic moment, a moment that we cannot afford to waste," McCaul said during debate. "We shared a fundamental belief that America is strongest at home when it projects strength abroad. This legislation does exactly that. EUROPE BANKROLLS PUTIN'S WAR MACHINE EVEN AS NATO RACES TO BOLSTER DEFENSES "It targets the money that fuels Russia's war machine. It sanctions Russian officials and oligarchs, banks and financial institutions and the shadow fleet that helps cheap Russian energy moving and through precisely targeted tariffs. It also punishes countries providing financial support for the deadliest war in Europe since World War II. Why? Because, as we've heard from President Zelenskyy's team, you can evade sanctions, which the Russians have done for years. But you cannot evade tariffs." The bill, which has gone through several iterations, still primarily focuses on kneecapping Putin’s war machine in Russia’s ongoing fight with Ukraine. US TARGETS CHINESE REFINERY IN SWEEPING IRAN OIL CRACKDOWN, SANCTIONS ‘SHADOW FLEET’ TANKERS But tweaks were needed to get sign-off from the White House. However, it reinserted sanctions targeting Iran’s weapons and energy sectors in the hopes of incentivizing a lasting peace deal as the war in the Middle East marches on. Key components of the legislation allow for up to 500% tariffs on Russian imports, and tariffs of up to 100% on the top five countries buying Russian energy. And it provides Trump flexibility for when to turn off some aspects of the sanctions. The tariff authority has proven a hard sell for House Democrats, though their colleagues in the Senate largely bought in. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., helped create the bill and largely spearheaded Democrat support in the Senate. PUTIN, RUSSIA PUT ON NOTICE AS SENATE TAKES CRUCIAL STEP TO GRIND DOWN THE KREMLIN’S WAR MACHINE Blumenthal defended the tariff language in the bill to Fox News Digital. "If Donald Trump wants to break this law, he will be restrained by the courts, just as when he broke the law on tariffs previously," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP It now heads to Trump's desk for his signature. At least two Democrats signaled early on that they would support the bill; Reps. Jared Golden, D-Maine, and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., defied their party leaders on Tuesday to help Republicans break gridlock on advancing the legislation. Their votes rescued the sanctions package from dying on the House floor amid a conservative rebellion over an unrelated issue. A similar move by the pair earlier this month earned a public reprimand from Jeffries, who called it a "breach of trust." "Congressman Golden has been a consistent supporter of America’s allies in Ukraine. He didn’t want to see the Russia sanctions bill die in a rule vote after passing with overwhelming bipartisan support in the Senate," Golden's spokesman told Fox News Digital of the vote.

articles.title: House passes Russia sanctions bill named for Lindsey Graham, sending it to Trump
articles.summary: The legislation, which passed the Senate last month, would target Russia’s energy sector by punishing the largest buyers of its oil and gas to slash revenues Russia uses to attack Ukraine.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The House voted Wednesday to pass a major bill aimed at imposing sanctions on Russia and Iran, sending it to President Donald Trump for his signature. The vote was 262-159. The 61-page legislation, which passed the Senate 86-11 last month, was named the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, in honor of the late senator, who was an outspoken proponent of the cause before his unexpected death in July. The bill takes aim at Russia’s energy sector by punishing the largest buyers of its oil and gas, allowing the president to impose tariffs on goods from those countries, which may include China and India. The goal: to slash the revenue streams that fund Russia’s ongoing war on Ukraine, which began in 2022. “The act’s most consequential new authority is its provision to place tariffs of up to 100 percent on third countries purchasing significant volumes of Russian energy,” according to the nonpartisan Center for Strategic and International Studies. “This replaces the blanket 500 percent tariff in the 2025 version with a more measured instrument, alongside a carve-out for countries taking significant steps to reduce dependence on Russian energy and whose imports amount to less than 15 percent of Russia’s annual natural gas exports.” The Atlantic Council said the bill would “authorize the Trump administration to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on Chinese imports on national security grounds if China continues purchasing Russian oil. This approach assumes that tariffs will compel China to reduce imports of Russian energy.” The measure would also target Russian government officials, as well as oligarchs, some family members and Russian financial institutions. At Trump’s request, the package would also extend sanction authority aimed at slashing funding for Iran’s weapons and energy sectors. Some top House Democrats criticized the bill, fretting that it would grant broad tariff authorities that Trump could abuse. But in the end, those hesitations weren’t enough to scuttle it. “I have always been in favor of the Russia sanctions bill,” House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told reporters Monday. “But we had to build a consensus around it, and I think we have it.” Daniel Balson of Razom for Ukraine, a U.S. advocacy group supporting Ukraine, called the bill’s passage “momentous.” “It comes as Russian officials move towards full-scale mobilization and intensify their bombing campaign against Ukraine’s critical energy infrastructure,” he said in a statement. “This bill sends an unmistakable message: for so long as Putin continues to inflict suffering on Ukraine, Congress will continue to impose consequences on Putin.”

articles.title: House passes Russia sanctions bill, handing Trump more leverage against Moscow
articles.summary: The vote ends a nearly two-year pause in Ukraine assistance from Congress.
articles.body:
The House passed the sweeping Russia sanctions bill long championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham on Wednesday, sending the legislation to the White House for President Donald Trump's signature after more than a year of congressional maneuvering.

The 262 to 159 vote ends a nearly two-year lull in Ukraine assistance from Congress, which had not passed any major Ukraine efforts since a 2024 emergency aid package. The bill faced a number of obstacles on the path to the Resolute Desk, including significant opposition from some House Democrats who argued that the bill would give the White House too much tariff power.

After weathering a number of storms to make it out of Capitol Hill, the legislation is all but guaranteed to get Trump's signature.

The long-anticipated legislation issues mandatory sanctions on Russia's leadership and energy sector — as well as new sanctions on collaborators in Moscow's defense industry and its so-called shadow fleet. Advocates of the bill, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, have argued it would give the White House necessary tools to squeeze Russia economically, curbing the flow of funds to Moscow's war machine.

But, to many Democrats' dismay, the legislation also includes a 100% tariff on top buyers of Russian energy. Opponents of the bill have cautioned that the tariff provision would hand another cudgel for Trump to use against not only U.S. foes but also global allies — an action the White House has repeatedly taken since Trump returned to office.

"We cannot grant more tariff power that we know he will abuse," Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.) said in comments on the House floor Wednesday.

Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, argued that the tariffs would worsen the economic pain already felt by everyday Americans and that without a security assistance package or more air defense, they would not do enough to concretely help Ukraine.

In comments on the House floor earlier Wednesday, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries outlined why he planned to withhold support for the measure.

"The manner in which this bill has been written doesn't require the president of the United States to impose sanctions on Russia," Jeffries said. "In fact, there are so many loopholes written into the bill, I believe, that it's very unlikely that the sanctions relief contemplated in the legislation will ever see the light of day."

That disagreement has caused a growing rift among Democrats in recent days. Fifty-eight House Democrats broke with Jeffries to vote yes on the measure.

In a letter addressed to House Democrats, Senate Foreign Relations ranking member Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) urged her colleagues to pass the legislation, warning that failing to do so would send a dangerous message to both Russian leader Vladimir Putin and other international foes.

"Congress's failure to impose additional costs would send a dangerous signal," Shaheen wrote. "The Kremlin is watching. Kyiv is watching. Our NATO allies are watching. So are Beijing, Tehran and Pyongyang."

articles.title: House passes bill to shield consumers from data center price hikes on energy
articles.summary: Under pressure to act on unpopular data centers, the House passed bipartisan legislation to shield consumers from higher energy costs.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Under pressure to act on unpopular data centers, the House on Wednesday overwhelmingly passed bipartisan legislation aimed at shielding consumers from higher energy costs when new data centers are built in their communities. The vote was nearly unanimous, 417-3, with the only opposition coming from progressive Reps. Summer Lee, D-Pa., Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., and Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich. Because GOP leaders brought the bill to the floor under a fast-tracking procedure known as suspension, support from two-thirds of voting lawmakers was required. The bill, dubbed the Ratepayers Protection Act, is the only legislation related to artificial intelligence that was scheduled for a vote this week as Congress considers its response to dire warnings from some former AI employees about its dangers. With the House holding its final votes before the midterm elections on Wednesday evening, and the Senate only staying in Washington a few more weeks, not much more is expected to get done to address the AI issue until at least the post-election lame-duck session. The data center bill was co-sponsored by Reps. Gabe Evans, R-Colo., and Kathy Castor, D-Fla., both members of the Energy and Commerce Committee. It aims to put the onus and responsibility on tech and data center companies — rather than consumers — to pay for power upgrades required to operate new large data centers. Specifically, the legislation would create a federal standard for state utility regulators to consider when creating rules for large, high-power data centers to cover the costs of power generation, transmission lines and other infrastructure upgrades needed to power these facilities, according to Evans. Data centers provide the computing power and storage for artificial intelligence. The Evans-Castor bill, however, does not address any of the recent warnings from AI researchers: that the fast-moving technology could cause human extinction. And it’s unclear what the Senate will do with the bill, if anything. The upper chamber has its own set of data center bills, but it hasn’t moved any. “Hardworking families should not have to subsidize the energy demands of data centers,” Evans said in a statement after the vote. “America needs the infrastructure to lead the world in AI and outcompete Communist China, but we cannot have that growth at the expense of hardworking families, farmers, seniors, and small businesses.” Evans, in his first term, is one of the most vulnerable House Republicans of the cycle; Cook Political Report characterized his race against Democratic state Rep. Manny Rutinel in Colorado as a “toss-up.” Evans and other at-risk lawmakers had been pressing GOP leaders for a vote on data centers, which have emerged as a key campaign issue in the November midterm elections. President Donald Trump has fully supported the construction of new data centers, saying they are critical for U.S.-based AI companies to compete with China. But voters in swing districts and swing states have argued that data centers are springing up across America too fast, and they’ve begun mobilizing against their construction in many places. A recent NBC News Decision Desk poll powered by SurveyMonkey found that nearly 70% of respondents oppose the construction of AI data centers in their neighborhood; 45% said they were strongly opposed. The ratepayer bill was just one of a handful of energy-related bills the House took up in its final week in session before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. The votes come as oil remains above $100 a barrel and the high cost of living and inflation remain the top issues heading into Election Day. Many Democrats supported the measure, saying they didn’t view the bill as harmful, but they panned it as weak. “Our communities and the people in our districts are so outraged, and they are understandably very angry that Congress isn’t doing enough” on data centers, Rep. Veronica Escobar, D-Texas, who represents El Paso, told NBC News before the vote. “I’m going to vote yes, but it is truly the bare minimum. In fact, it’s kind of pathetic that all we’re going to do is make them pay their own energy costs.” “These data centers are going into communities like mine that don’t want them,” she added. “My community does not want data centers, loudly and clearly, and I agree with my community.” Michigan Rep. Debbie Dingell, who heads Democrats’ policy and communications arm, voted yes but said, “It’s not enough in any way, shape or form.” And former Progressive Caucus Chairwoman Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., who also supported the bill, pointed to Trump’s comments this week that the AI industry doesn’t need guardrails and that serious safety warnings about AI are a “hoax.” “This is the same party that has a president that says that the AI threat is a hoax, and so I am worried about just allowing this to be, ‘Oh, we’ve solved it,’” Jayapal said. The effort “is a direct contradiction to what their president is continuing to say in opposing any real regulation.”
