articles.title: Trump bashes Democrats on crime while campaigning for Michael Whatley in North Carolina
articles.summary: Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman, faces Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper in a critical race for the Senate.
articles.body: GASTONIA, N.C. — President Donald Trump leaned heavily into law and order as he worked to build support for the Republican candidate in a North Carolina race that could decide which party controls the Senate for the back half of his second term. Speaking at an airport rally Wednesday, Trump said Democrats coddle criminals, peppering his hourlong speech with graphic details of violent crimes that he said are an outgrowth of Democratic policies. He used visual aids to draw visceral reactions aimed at stoking antipathy to the Democratic candidate, former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper. At one point, an oversize video screen displayed mug shots of unnamed criminal suspects. The Republican running against Cooper, Michael Whatley, will make the streets safer, Trump said. “You can either vote for Roy Cooper to set loose criminals who rape and murder your children and your population, or you can vote for Michael Whatley to protect and defend your children and your population,” Trump said. One of the speakers who preceded Trump was Todd Blanche, the U.S. attorney general. It’s a break from tradition for the attorney general to appear at partisan political rallies, but Trump has eroded some of the post-Watergate norms that sought to insulate the nation’s top law enforcement officer from politics. Trump’s trip to North Carolina is his third since December in support of Whatley’s campaign. A lot rides on the outcome. The North Carolina seat is now held by Republican Thom Tillis, a Trump critic who is retiring. Democrats must net four seats in the November elections to capture the Senate majority. Cooper was leading Whatley by 11 percentage points in the latest Elon University poll of likely voters. That makes North Carolina ripe for a potential Democratic pickup. Whatley is tying his candidacy tightly to Trump. Trump won North Carolina in all three of his presidential campaigns, even as Cooper won the governorship in 2016 and 2020; Whatley needs Trump to energize the MAGA base. Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chairman, lacks the name recognition in the state that Cooper enjoys as a former two-term governor. He also faces a fundraising disadvantage. Cooper’s campaign had nearly $21 million to spend as of June 30, while Whatley’s campaign had $3.5 million, according to the most recent campaign finance reports. Trump praised Whatley throughout the speech. In his own brief remarks before Trump took the stage, Whatley mentioned Trump’s name repeatedly. “President Trump needs an ally who will work to lower costs, protect our families and preserve the American dream,” he said. Polling shows that crime isn’t a top-of-mind concern for most voters across the U.S. Crime and safety have consistently ranked behind the economy, threats to democracy and healthcare in NBC News polls of U.S. adults asked to name the issue that matters most to them over the last year. But Trump and North Carolina Republicans see crime as a vulnerability for Cooper. Trump devoted part of his speech to a 23-year-old Ukrainian woman, Iryna Zarutska, who was stabbed to death last year on a commuter train in Charlotte. “You worked your entire life for everything you have,” Trump said. “You saved your money, followed the law, and now Roy Cooper and his band of communists want to take everything you have and give it to people who would rob your house, invade your border, just shoot you dead.” Trump also used the speech to reassure voters who are squeezed by high fuel costs. Gas prices have spiked since the Trump administration and Israel launched an attack on Iran on Feb. 28. The price hike is temporary, Trump said. “It’s a very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done,” he said. “Remember that. It’s a little more. Frankly, even if it was a lot more. But that’s going to be coming tumbling down. That’s going to be like a rocket ship in reverse.”

articles.title: 20 states sue to block Trump admin rule that would make it harder for immigrants to obtain visas, green cards
articles.summary: More than 20 states sued the Department of Homeland Security over a public charge rule that could increase green card denials based on Medicaid and SNAP use.
articles.body: More than 20 states are suing the Trump administration over a new Department of Homeland Security rule that would give immigration officials wider discretion in determining what constitutes a public charge, a statute that allows the government to deny visas or green cards to applicants it determines are likely to become dependent on government assistance. The rule, which is set to take effect on Friday, would expand the list of possible government aid that officials could point to when deciding to disqualify an applicant. New York State Attorney General Letitia James led a coalition of 21 states and Washington, D.C., in suing the administration over what they describe as punishment for immigrants' law use of public assistance. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani led a separate lawsuit filed by a coalition of cities challenging DHS' rule. James said the rule would allow immigration officials to consider an immigrant's use of benefits like Medicaid, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and participation in school meal programs when determining whether they could become dependent on government aid. She also said it could lead to more fear of interacting with the government for people who are part of an immigrant family. TRUMP ADMIN PAUSES VISA APPOINTMENTS WORLDWIDE AMID HEIGHTENED SCREENING FOR APPLICANTS "Hardworking families should not be forced to go without the support they need because they fear asking for assistance will get them deported," James said in a statement. "This rule preys on that fear and counts on families forfeiting the food assistance, health care coverage, and other public benefits to which they are legally entitled. My office fought this exact policy once before and won, and we are leading the nation to ensure the Trump administration cannot inflict this harm on families again." The public charge ground applies to certain immigrants seeking admission or adjustment of status. Most undocumented immigrants are ineligible for federal means-tested public benefits, although limited exceptions exist under federal and state law. The states argue they would lose billions of dollars in federal funding if immigrants pull from programs over fears about the public charge rule. Immigration officials under the Biden administration's 2022 public charge rule generally considered only cash assistance for income maintenance, such as Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) or Supplemental Security Income (SSI), along with government-funded long-term institutionalization, when determining a public charge. The rule does not specify a fixed list of public benefits that immigration officials may consider. Instead, it states that officers may consider the receipt of any means-tested public benefits as part of a public charge determination, giving them broader discretion in evaluating applicants. The states' and cities' lawsuits asked the courts to declare the rule unlawful and prevent DHS from using it. "It's very hard to predict how courts will look at this issue. It is very unusual regulation though," Cato Institute Director of Immigration Studies David Bier told Fox News Digital. "I think from that standpoint the states have a good argument that we had a well defined public charge rule and the administration didn't replace it with some other well defined rule, it replaced it with nothing. So now there's just discretion to the officers to do whatever they want with the underlying statute. There's no regulation that clearly says this is what it means to be a public charge in the United States." "The rule as it was before this new regulation was you had to be primarily dependent on certain government benefit programs. This rule removes that definition and doesn't replace it with anything. So now people and applicants, lawyers who are applying to the government on behalf of applicants, they don't know really what the law is," he continued. The states' lawsuit argues that DHS is exceeding its authority because Congress did not approve a broader interpretation of what it means to be a public charge. The states say the new rule is arbitrary and that the agency ignored the harmful consequences of the change. DOJ THREATENS TO CUT BILLIONS IN WELFARE FUNDING FROM STATES FOR FAILING TO REPORT ILLEGAL MIGRANTS "Cruelty is the point," James said at a press conference on Monday. "Having a chilling effect on immigrants is the point. Letting individuals know that they are not welcome here is the point. Immigration animus is the point. The fact that you’re going to deny individuals who are sick and hungry and homeless benefits just is beyond the pale." DHS did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment in time for publication. Bier said the rule does not prohibit immigrants from receiving welfare and is only used as an officer's projection about someone's likelihood of future welfare use in the U.S., warning that it could lead to self-sufficient applicants being denied. "Whether someone is currently using benefits or not doesn't matter under this evaluation. It's this probabilistic determination of the future that they're using in order to deny people legal status and legal permanent resident status in the United States. That's a much more difficult assessment to make. That's going to result in arbitrary denials. It's just not possible to do this type of assessment and not result in people who would be self-sufficient being denied status," he said. This comes as President Donald Trump pursues a broader immigration crackdown that has extended beyond illegal immigration to legal immigration pathways. While Trump campaigned in 2024 on curbing illegal immigration, his administration has also imposed additional restrictions on legal immigration, including higher fees for certain work visas and new limits on how long some foreign students and journalists can remain in the U.S. The administration has also pursued visa revocations and removal proceedings in cases involving political activity and speech, including some anti-Israel activists. Those efforts have prompted court challenges in which plaintiffs allege violations of First Amendment free speech and Fifth Amendment due process protections. "It's very clear that this administration wants to restrict both illegal immigration, which obviously it's done at the border, and through deportations, but also legal immigration," Bier said. Last month, the administration directed U.S. embassies and consulates around the world to postpone immigrant visa interviews while consular officers complete training on new public charge guidance, temporarily stalling applications that had reached the interview stage. "The primary population that's going to be affected by this public charge rule are spouses of U.S. citizens and their kids who are trying to receive green cards so they can live with their American spouse or parent here in the United States. That's the overwhelming majority of the people who are going to be affected by the rule. It's going to result in many of those immigrant families being separated from their American spouse or parent," Bier said. MAMDANI BLASTS FEDS FOR WAGING 'CAMPAIGN OF VIOLENCE AND TERROR' AGAINST NYC'S IMMIGRANTS The public charge provision stems from the Immigration Act of 1882, when federal lawmakers sought to ensure that immigrants would be able to take care of themselves and not become a public burden. After years of only considering cash benefits, the first Trump administration widened the categories of benefit programs that could be considered a public charge, including Medicaid, food stamps and housing vouchers. But the Biden administration in 2022 published a rule that returned to the previous guidance. The rule set to take effect this week would rescind the Biden administration's rule. The new rule is more broad than the one from the first Trump administration, as it does not specify which safety nets should be considered and only states that DHS "will consider the receipt of any means tested public benefits." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "One of the most important things to understand is that during the first Trump administration, they had a public charge rule that was well defined that really did explain exactly what you were supposed to do in order to not be deemed a public charge or who was a public charge. This is completely different from that. It's essentially the Wild West. No one knows what's going on, no one knows what the law is now," Bier said.

articles.title: House races for exit, avoiding vote on Hegseth impeachment
articles.summary: House lawmakers raced for the exits on Wednesday, trimming their final week in Washington ahead of the midterm elections and kicking a controversial vote to impeach Pete Hegseth into the lame duck session. House GOP leaders scrapped votes scheduled for Thursday, when the resolution to remove the Defense secretary was expected to hit the floor.…
articles.body:
House lawmakers raced for the exits on Wednesday, trimming their final week in Washington ahead of the midterm elections and kicking a controversial vote to impeach Pete Hegseth into the lame duck session.

House GOP leaders scrapped votes scheduled for Thursday, when the resolution to remove the Defense secretary was expected to hit the floor.

The move sent lawmakers onto the campaign trail a day early, as both parties race for House control next year. And it fixed in place the legislative accomplishments Republicans are able to tout heading into those elections, leaving a number of their policy priorities stewing in the Senate.

But it was the Hegseth issue getting the most attention. The impeachment push, which Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) unveiled on Tuesday , had caught Republicans off guard and GOP leaders were eager to avoid a vote that might hurt lawmakers in tough races. Democrats and Massie quickly accused GOP leaders of vacating Thursday’s session to avoid that vote.

“And there it is. Just as I predicted. They’re canceling Congress tomorrow to avoid the vote on IMPEACHING @SecWar ,” Massie, a vocal critic of the Trump White House, wrote on X.

“These people are such incredible cowards,” Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) said in a video clip, referring to Republicans. “Mike Johnson and Donald Trump are so afraid that the Republicans and Democrats in Congress would vote for that resolution of impeachment and that it would pass because they know that what Pete Hegseth has done, his role in driving us into this war, is absolutely wrong, and he needs to be held accountable for it.”

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) quickly dismissed the criticisms, telling reporters that it’s “ridiculous” to suggest GOP leaders altered the schedule to avoid a tough vote. He called Massie’s move a “publicity stunt by someone who wants attention,” predicting the impeachment resolution will “immediately” be rejected in the lame duck.

“It’s a stunt. Secretary Hegseth has done an extraordinary job, the Department of War. We’re in the middle of international conflicts right now, and we should not be playing games with national security. And I think that’s how the members see this,” Johnson said.

It’s hardly unusual for Congress to take a long break heading into elections. The difference this year was that both chambers were able to approve a massive federal spending package in early September, rather than creeping closer to the Oct. 1 shutdown deadline, as is more typically the case.

With a shutdown averted, Johnson had canceled the last two weeks of the September session earlier this month, arguing that much of the GOP’s remaining legislative agenda has been stalled in the Senate and that lawmakers could use the extra time to campaign.

“Right now, it almost feels like a pointless exercise for us to continue sending and stacking legislation over there, when members could be in their districts campaigning in this very fateful moment,” Johnson said Tuesday. “That’s a critically important thing.”

Johnson said that if the Senate begins to move on legislation, he will bring “everybody back and we’ll get it all going.”

The early departure also fueled the partisan clash over artificial intelligence (AI), as Democrats urged Johnson to keep the House in session to implement bipartisan AI safeguards. That push intensified following warnings from some AI giants about the risk of global catastrophe if the technology evolves too quickly. Democrats see a strong role for Congress in adopting industry guardrails, while Johnson wants the tech companies to spearhead that process.

There’s no chance Congress would have reached a consensus on AI restrictions ahead of the elections. But given the public anxieties on the issue, Democrats are highlighting Congress’s early exodus to bash Republicans for not even trying.

“We believe in having a reasonable regulatory framework, and it’s clear that these companies, the frontier companies themselves, are asking for this,” said Rep. Pete Aguilar (Calif.), chairman of the House Democratic Caucus. “This is something that Congress should lead in. And what Speaker Johnson is doing is abdicating his authority.”

Some conservatives are also up in arms over the House’s early exit.

Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.), a member of the far-right House Freedom Caucus who lost the South Carolina GOP gubernatorial and special Senate primaries, wrote on X that canceling another day of votes is “unacceptable.”

“The House has now canceled at least 63 scheduled voting days this Congress, including nine days this month alone, and now we’re leaving Washington until after the election. The Founders did not envision taking this much time off and still getting paid,” he wrote.

“If Members of Congress want to go home and campaign instead of doing the job taxpayers sent us here to do, then their campaigns ought to be paying them, NOT the American taxpayer,” he added. “We still have work to do.”

With the House now gone, much of that work will be kicked to the lame duck, which is scheduled to begin on Nov. 9. The tone of that session will hinge largely on the results of the midterms, when both the House and Senate are up for grabs. If Democrats flip control of at least one chamber, as some handicappers are predicting, it would heighten the urgency among Republicans to advance their remaining priorities before the power shift in 2027.

A number of those bills are lingering in the Senate, including a proposal to regulate cryptocurrency , dubbed the Clarity Act; legislation to reauthorize food and agricultural programs for the next five years, known as the Farm Bill; and a $95 billion reconciliation package that Republicans have sought to move unilaterally.

That partisan package includes $10 billion in incentives for states to adopt tougher election rules — an idea championed by Trump — and $73 billion in new funding for the Iran War, a topic some Republicans wanted to avoid before the midterms.

The Hegseth impeachment resolution ensures that the Iran issue will be front-and-center in the earliest days of the House’s return. Of the eight impeachment articles, four of them pertain to Hegseth’s conduct of the war, which Massie deems illegal because Congress hasn’t authorized it.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) could also be in a tough spot if Democrats win the House, as the Massie resolution could force him to tiptoe the line between wanting to have a better relationship with the White House and Republicans versus standing up more aggressively to Trump officials, which some progressives in the party have called for.

articles.title: Kennedy Center faces uncertain future after Trump closure
articles.summary: The fight over the Kennedy Center is not slowing down after President Trump made planned renovations contingent on his name appearing on the building while a Trump-aligned board voted to close the venue down. Federal judge Christopher Cooper has blocked both efforts, but fencing went up around the main building Wednesday, which was closed to…
articles.body:
The fight over the Kennedy Center is not slowing down after President Trump made planned renovations contingent on his name appearing on the building while a Trump-aligned board voted to close the venue down.

Federal judge Christopher Cooper has blocked both efforts, but fencing went up around the main building Wednesday, which was closed to the public.

Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex officio board member who has repeatedly challenged the Kennedy Center board’s moves, asked a federal judge on Wednesday to call an emergency hearing for an explanation about the center’s closure.

The request noted that a staff member for one of the law firms representing Beatty attempted to enter the Kennedy Center that morning but was turned away by security. She was told, according to court filings, that construction on the interior of the building was underway, and it was not open to the public.

“Closing the Kennedy Center without Judge Cooper’s approval appears to directly violate his order. This is an assault on the rule of law,” attorneys Nathaniel Zelinsky and Norm Eisen said in a separate statement. “The board cannot simply ignore Judge Cooper’s rulings whenever it suits them. In this country, no one — including the president — is above the law.”

The Justice Department has been ordered to respond by Thursday morning. Beatty’s legal team wants a “high-level decisionmaker” at the Kennedy Center to be there if a hearing happens.

The escalation came less than a day after Cooper ruled that the board cannot move forward with its latest attempt to inscribe Trump’s name on the building without “Congress’s blessing.” It was the second time he had said no to the Trump name addition, having previously ordered in late May that Trump’s name be stripped from the facade.

Shortly after that ruling, the board voted to immediately shutter the main building.

Beatty revealed later that she and Trump got into a heated discussion during the vote, and the president called her names.

“He has a limited vocabulary, so, you know, he knows words like ‘dumb,’ you know, and things like that. I was surprised that the board people let it go on. So, we had some exchange of words,” she told NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network.

The president and the board have maintained that the closure is needed for repairs. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick posted a video of a piece of ceiling collapsing.

Resolutions from the board had pointed to Trump’s fundraising skills as the only way to save the building, presenting different options for how his contribution could be recognized. The president said in a Truth Social post that $17 million in donations had been put into the performing arts center account to “keep it afloat.”

But Congress appropriated roughly $257 million to cover the needed repairs just last year, with much of it made available through 2029.

“That pot of money is completely adequate, and his refusal to spend it is really the equivalent of going on strike,” said David Super, a law professor at Georgetown University. “It’s just an act of defiance. It has no legal basis at all, and it violates his statutory duties as one of the Kennedy Center’s trustees.”

“I don’t know where this comes from, other than extortion,” he added.

A White House official defended the closure, saying the center will be closed for “at least seven days.”

“Two weeks ago, a large portion of ceiling collapsed into the Kennedy Center. In order to protect the public from falling debris and other dangers, the Kennedy Center will be temporarily close for at least seven days to permit a safety evaluation and to secure public visitors against other risks,” they said. “This temporary safety-related closure is distinct from the closure on which the Board recently voted, and on which we are awaiting a ruling from the D.C. court.”

But Trump said in his Truth Social post Tuesday that the renovations and repairs won’t begin unless the court approves the board’s plan to put his name on the building.

Cooper’s initial order had allowed “necessary maintenance and repair work” to continue but barred a prolonged closure.

There’s not much more the board could do in terms of getting Trump’s name added to the building, besides getting Congress to amend the Kennedy Center statute. Super said he doesn’t see lawmakers or the Supreme Court siding with the board.

“The odds of that passing Congress, I think, are fairly remote,” he said. “I think even Republicans would be embarrassed by that, and Democrats really would filibuster.”

As for the legal options, Super said Cooper could issue a more specific order, potentially appoint an independent official to act as oversight or hold board members in contempt if the court’s orders aren’t followed.

“Frankly, I see it finishing either with a receiver being appointed to take over it, or with Trump sending a wrecking ball over there,” he said.

articles.title: The Memo: Trump’s AI advocacy lands with a thud, even among some in GOP
articles.summary: President Trump has long prided himself on his ability to instinctively sense the views of the public on a whole range of hot-button issues. But some in his own party are worried that he may be dramatically out of step on two intertwined issues that have suddenly become central to the national debate: artificial intelligence…
articles.body:
President Trump has long prided himself on his ability to instinctively sense the views of the public on a whole range of hot-button issues.

But some in his own party are worried that he may be dramatically out of step on two intertwined issues that have suddenly become central to the national debate: artificial intelligence and the data centers that power it.

Trump has repeatedly expressed enthusiasm for these new developments. He has even — and often — argued that those who are criticizing the nascent industry are engaging in a “hoax.”

On Monday alone, he unleashed a barrage of social media messages defending AI and lambasting the warnings of significant downsides to the growth of the industry.

In one characteristically ebullient post, the president wrote, “AI, and Data Centers, will be the Greatest Economic Development Engine in History ­­— Bigger than Oil, Gold, Diamonds, or even the Internet. It will not be stopped by brilliantly run Destructive Forces during the Term of President DONALD J. TRUMP!”

In another, he equated people sounding warnings about AI and data centers to environmental activists who warn about climate change. Trump has long been skeptical of climate change, despite the overwhelming weight of scientific evidence showing its baleful effects.

The anti-AI forces, Trump contended, are “Revolutionaries, but Revolutionaries for a Bad and Evil Cause.”

Perhaps most substantive — and most controversial — was yet another post in which Trump contended there was no real need for further regulation of AI, at least so long as he is at the helm.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” he wrote. “We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies!”

Notably, many in his party have seemed significantly less enthused about these issues.

Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), for example, has pushed legislation to compel tech companies to cover some of the costs of data center infrastructure as he fights a competitive battle against his Democratic challenger, former Sen. Sherrod Brown (Ohio).

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has tried to navigate an even more delicate course, expressing largely noncommittal or “middle ground” sentiments.

“There’s a lot of opinions on this,” Johnson told reporters earlier this week. “Obviously there’s a need for guardrails, but there’s also a keen need for the industry to self-regulate and self-monitor and report to us.”

It’s a difficult spot for many Republicans. They are caught between two pincers: a president who regularly sounds like an AI evangelist and an electorate that has surprised many pundits with the depth of its hostility to the new, exponentially growing industry.

In particular, the growth of data centers has proven even more controversial than AI itself. Much of the media coverage of the centers has emphasized the vast resources used.

A new University of Massachusetts Amherst poll released this week found that a mere 11 percent of Americans would support an AI data center being built in their area, while 65 percent would oppose such a development.

In a statement accompanying the release, the university noted, “Republicans are more receptive than Democrats, but even Republicans oppose a data center in their community by nearly 3-1, 52 percent to 18 percent.”

The extent to which the issue crosses party lines was seen in even more concrete form early this week, as left-wing icon Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and MAGA stalwart Steve Bannon both attended a “pro-human” conference where warnings about AI’s dangers were the order of the day.

These same dynamics are causing real headaches, including for Republican strategists, on all sides of the AI debate.

Liz Mair, a longtime Republican strategist, is a strong believer in the potential of AI.

But Mair told this column that she believes many of the companies working in the area are underestimating the level of public skepticism — and the extent to which it could put the brakes on their activity. She further worries that Trump is so inherently divisive a figure that his vocal and frequent expressions of support could boomerang, causing opposition to rise.

“I basically agree with him 100 percent on this,” Mair said. “The thing that is therefore frustrating is that this is a guy who has terrible approval ratings. If he came out and said ‘water is wet’ you would run the risk of 60 percent of the country saying, ‘Nuh-uh, it’s dry.’ I would prefer if he was not talking about this at all.”

Brendan Steinhauser is also a Republican strategist but one who wears a second hat as the CEO of the Alliance for Secure AI, which describes itself as part of an effort to “educate the public about the implications of advanced AI.”

Steinhauser argued that Trump sees AI almost entirely through the lens of something that could help bolster the nation’s economy.

But he’s not sure the public agrees — and emphasizes there are political ramifications to that.

The economic upside “is where his head is at, but what he has been saying about data centers and AI just hasn’t got through,” Steinhauser argued. “It could very well be a problem for the president politically and for Republicans running across the country for House and Senate.”

Steinhauser said GOP operatives across the country sometimes share their polling or focus group data on the emerging tech with him.

“The numbers for data centers are atrocious, and the numbers for AI itself are not far behind,” he said.

For now, Trump seems set on his staunchly pro-AI line.

But even some pro-AI voices, like Mair, worry about whether the president will hold fast to his current position if he keeps running into winds of resistance among his own supporters.

“The biggest MAGA types and the people who have gone most to the mat to defend Trump are not people who agree with him on this,” she said. “My worry is that I’m not actually sure Trump stays in the lane that he is in right now.”

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: Iran war puts future US military presence in Middle East in question
articles.summary: America’s war against Iran is stirring debate inside and outside the U.S. government over the future presence of the U.S. military in the Middle East. Following the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks, the U.S. built up a massive configuration of military bases and intelligence outposts in the region to launch strikes, disrupt terrorists and wage…
articles.body:
America’s war against Iran is stirring debate inside and outside the U.S. government over the future presence of the U.S. military in the Middle East.

Following the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks, the U.S. built up a massive configuration of military bases and intelligence outposts in the region to launch strikes, disrupt terrorists and wage wars.

But the ongoing conflict with Tehran has shed light on the susceptibility of U.S. military infrastructure in the Gulf, as many of those bases have sustained heavy damage from Iranian drone and missile attacks.

That’s become a key factor in informal discussions about potential cuts to the U.S. military presence, which began before President Trump launched attacks on Iran.

The ultimate decision around the withdrawal of U.S. troops in the Middle East hinges on the outcome of the war with Iran, according to multiple people familiar with conversations in and around the Pentagon, who spoke to The Hill on condition of anonymity.

Allison Minor, who was the director for Arabian Peninsula affairs on the National Security Council during Trump’s first term, said forces within the administration view a reduced presence as a “necessary recalibration,” regardless of the conflict with Iran and its proxies.

However, damage to U.S. bases in the Middle East has made a drawdown all but inevitable, Jennifer Kavanagh, a senior fellow and director of military analysis at Defense Priorities, said in an interview.

About 70 structures at 11 U.S. military bases in the Middle East have sustained $5 billion in damage, the American Enterprise Institute said in a report in late April.

Iran’s attacks have damaged and destroyed “hundreds of buildings and structures” at U.S. military bases in Kuwait, Jordan, Oman, Qatar, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, a Monday Pentagon watchdog report said.

“I think the reality is that even if the Pentagon would like to keep military forces in the Middle East after the war, the bases around the Persian Gulf, in places like Bahrain and Qatar and Kuwait, are simply not defensible,” Kavanagh said.

“They’ve been badly damaged during the war, so they would have to be rebuilt, and it’s pretty clear that if they were rebuilt, there would be a high risk they’d be damaged again in future conflicts.”

Asked for comment, a U.S. official with Central Command (Centcom), the combatant command that oversees U.S. forces in the Middle East, said: “We will not speculate on future force posture for operational security reasons.”

The White House said the U.S. military “maintains the force posture necessary to achieve any desired objective set by” President Trump.

“As Operation Epic Fury demonstrated, America’s military might is stronger than it’s ever been,” White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement.

A Pentagon official told The Hill last month that the department “routinely conducts prudent monitoring and assessment” of U.S. force posture across the globe, and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has motioned for a formal review of the U.S. military footprint in the Middle East.

The analysis should consider what access the U.S. military needs to be able to sustain, what intelligence collection Washington requires, human relationships with regional allies, how the security relationships with those countries can evolve and how to best push back against Iranian threats, former national security officials said.

“From a tradecraft standpoint, you got to make sure that you realize that sometimes the intelligence you get from partners is not only provided to inform; sometimes it’s provided to influence, and so you’ve got to realize that as well, because sometimes we’re not willing to accept the risk of someone else getting it,” a former senior U.S. intelligence official, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly, told The Hill. “We have to get it ourselves firsthand, and so all of that plays into the calculus of how you figure out.”

The number of U.S. troops in the Centcom region went up in the few years prior to the 9/11 attacks and swelled as the Pentagon broadened its presence during the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.

Those in favor of maintaining a heavy military presence in the Centcom region have said it gives the U.S. access to basing and overflight, helps maintain air superiority over adversaries and maintains the ability to collect valuable intelligence.

In recent years, there have been growing calls to reduce the U.S. military footprint in the Middle East, with some arguing service members are vulnerable targets and that maintaining the bases isn’t worth the cost.

The U.S. currently has more than 50,000 service members in the Centcom region, stationed across the Middle East from Jordan to Oman. Those U.S. bases have come under fire since the Iran war broke out in late February, including Naval Support Activity Bahrain (NASB), which serves as the headquarters for U.S. Naval Forces Central Command and the U.S. Fifth Fleet.

“We’ve seen a level of risk in proximity, and we’ve also built this presence against the CT [counterterrorism] fight over the course, and then we’ve just increased the footprint and increased, and just got comfortable with an oversized footprint,” the ex-senior U.S. intelligence official said.

Last year, Kavanagh proposed closing U.S. bases in Kuwait and placing U.S. service members in Jordan, the UAE and Bahrain in facilities like the Prince Sultan Air Base near Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

Others who are more hawkish on Iran have suggested having U.S. forces moved to Ovda Air Base in Israel.

“Israel’s geostrategic location at the crossroads of Europe, Asia, and Africa enables it to support U.S. rapid global mobility by hosting tanker and transport aircraft,” the Jewish Institute for National Security of America (JINSA) wrote in a late March report .

Jonathan Ruhe, a fellow for American strategy at JINSA, said there is a “general atmosphere” in conversations with current and former officials that the U.S. position in the region is going to “have to change,” both in how forces are protected and how the military stores munitions in the region.

“To the extent we continue having permanent presences at fixed locations close to Iran, it’s just going to be [an] unsustainable proposition going forward,” Ruhe said in an interview.

Ruhe said the move to Ovda, located in the south of Israel, could relocate troops from Qatar and Jordan and some from Iraq and Saudi Arabia.

Some of the discussions around how to better defend U.S. positions in the Middle East include having some installations underground for greater deterrence, an idea that has been floated within the Pentagon in years prior.

“If we’re talking about completely building up new installations underground, those are significant expenses. So again, just thinking about what our presence in the region is going to be long term before we get to those investments,” Minor, now the director of the Atlantic Council’s Project for Middle East Integration, told The Hill.

Kavanagh said hardening of U.S. bases is a likely necessary step for future military operations, but placing them underground could complicate the usage of some assets.

“Now, it does complicate operations. If your assets are stored underground, that can complicate actually using them. Using both physical hardening above ground as new types of air defense and underground facilities, I think will be the way of the future, not just in the Middle East but globally.”

The U.S. military having a permanent presence at locations close to Iran while protecting it with more air defense systems is “not going to be a solution” because all service branches are concerned about depleting interceptor stocks, added Ruhe.

“That’s the tenor of the conversations we’ve been hearing since the war,” he said.

articles.title: Trump had to crush Iran instead of making deals. He didn’t — now he pays the price.
articles.summary: Last April, President Trump scolded Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on warfare. Trump told Zelensky, “When you start a war, you got to know you can win.” That advice was inapt to begin with — Ukraine didn’t start the defensive war in which it is now engaged — but it has aged especially poorly. Trump started a war with Iran this…
articles.body:
Last April, President Trump scolded Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on warfare. Trump told Zelensky, “When you start a war, you got to know you can win.”

That advice was inapt to begin with — Ukraine didn’t start the defensive war in which it is now engaged — but it has aged especially poorly.

Trump started a war with Iran this February. Now, 201 days later, he is still trying to figure out how to win. And of course, knowing you can win a war is not enough. Training, preparation, overwhelming force and violence of action win wars. By the time the order is given to the military to fight and win, all probable outcomes must have been wargamed and branches and sequels developed to counter them.

Equally as important to knowing how to win is knowing the enemy, as Sun Tzu famously wrote. The enemy always gets a vote, but “ you improvise, you overcome, you adapt .” You do not hit the pause button to see if the enemy has had enough yet or to make a deal. Momentum is a force-multiplier, and start and stop tactics are the enemy of momentum.

At the onset of Operation Epic Fury, the assumption Trump made was that Iranians would rise up and “take back their country” once the upper tier of Iranian leadership had been killed. They did not — not because they did not want to, but because conditions had not been set. Adm. Brad Cooper of U.S. Central Command repeatedly urged Iranian civilians to stay in their homes as U.S. and Israeli airstrikes targeted military infrastructure.

The Basij paramilitary remained intact — the force that executed a brutal and unprecedented crackdown on protesters in January, killing as many as 36,500 civilians and arresting over 1,500 .

At day 38 of the war, Trump tried to negotiate a ceasefire with Iran when it was clear the remaining second and third tier leadership were not going to capitulate to his demand of “unconditional surrender” to air power alone. His negotiating team of Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner practically committed to give Iran’s regime $600 billion in a 14-point memorandum of understanding to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Iran squandered that opportunity by firing on ships attempting to transit the Strait.

The White House has since shifted tactics. Economics became the instrument of national power of choice via Operation Economic Outcast . The military instrument — enforcement of a naval blockade — became the supporting effort to make the Iranian economy collapse.

But Iran had another card up its sleeve — its proxies. Shi’a militias in Iraq on Saturday attacked Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, the chief alternative to sending oil through the Strait of Hormuz. Then on Sunday, Houthi rebels seized Yemen’s Red Sea coastline and the strategic island of Mayyun, once again threatening freedom of navigation and the flow of international commercial shipping through the Red Sea.

The strait between the Red Sea and the Arabian Sea, known as the Bab al-Mandeb, handles roughly 12 percent of global trade, including 11 percent of maritime oil and 8 percent of liquefied natural gas.

With the East-West oil pipeline shut down and the Bab al-Mandeb under threat of Houthi attacks, the squeeze was back on the global oil market — Iran’s only source of leverage.

So Trump has now effectively started or restarted two wars, however you want to count them them. He has not committed to seeing either to conclusion, despite having the best trained, equipped and lethal military in the world at his disposal to execute the mission. He stopped Operation Rough Rider against the Houthis on day 52 and Operation Epic Fury on day 38.

But if he wants to defeat Iran’s regime, he must attack its center of gravity — in this case, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Instead, despite being on the brink of victory, Trump has repeatedly opted to negotiate ceasefires and peace deals with inexperienced and naive businessmen at the helm. This has offered our adversaries time, space, and finances not only to reset and resume their nefarious activities but even to expand the war.

Trump should have someone more qualified sit across the table from Houthi and Iranian negotiators — perhaps Cooper, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, CIA Director John Ratcliffe, or Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine.

They would deliver a clear ultimatum — “this is what you will do” — rather than ask, “What will it take?” Negotiations should carry real pressure, with consequences for any failure by Iran to keep its word.

The Trump administration learned another lesson last week: Cease-fires do not end wars. They merely set conditions to resume the fighting. Instead of to finish what you started.

Col. (Ret.) Jonathan Sweet served 30 years as a military intelligence officer and led the U.S. European Command Intelligence Engagement Division from 2012 to 2014. Mark Toth writes on national security and foreign policy. They are the co-founders of INTREP360 and the INTREP360 Intelligence Report on Substack.

articles.title: Fed interest rate hike adds to midterm tremors for GOP
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Fed raises interest rates after three-year pause ▪ House leaves Washington ahead of midterms ▪ Ovechkin’s ties to Putin under scrutiny ▪ Iowa emerging as key battleground The Federal Reserve raised interest rates yesterday for the first time since July 2023, a clear sign that central bank officials remain concerned about…
articles.body:
▪ Fed raises interest rates after three-year pause

▪ House leaves Washington ahead of midterms

▪ Ovechkin’s ties to Putin under scrutiny

The Federal Reserve raised interest rates yesterday for the first time since July 2023, a clear sign that central bank officials remain concerned about persistent inflation less than two months before the midterm elections.

The Federal Open Market Committee voted unanimously to raise its benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point, to a range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent. The latest projections suggest another increase could follow by the end of the year.

“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said Wednesday.

The move is intended to help cool inflation in the long-run, but consumers are more likely to notice rising borrowing costs in the short-term.

Credit card holders may find themselves paying a few extra dollars each month on their debt, while prospective home and car buyers could face higher quotes, according to Matt Schulz , LendingTree’s chief consumer finance analyst.

“This isn’t going to hit anybody super hard ,” Schulz told Morning Report. “But the people who are going to feel this the most are the people who have very little financial wiggle room right now. And so many people are living on tight budgets, living paycheck to paycheck, that every dollar matters.”

“If you are somebody who doesn’t really have much savings and has a pretty substantial amount of credit card debt, this could be noticeable for you,” Schulz added.

Schulz noted that the interest-rate hike is “good news for savers,” who could earn higher returns on money held in high-yield savings and money-market accounts.

While the increase may not have a substantial impact on most voters’ wallets, it could reinforce broader concerns about the economy and inflation heading into the midterms.

Francesco Trebbi , a professor of business and public policy at the University of California, Berkeley’s Haas School of Business, said the decision could put Republicans, who control Congress and the White House, in a difficult position heading into the midterms. He pointed to his research on the 2024 election, which found that declining purchasing power made voters more likely to vote against the incumbent.

“In order for the Fed hike to improve the inflation scenario, it will need to cool down the economy and somewhat depress aggregate demand,” Trebbi said. “ This will be potentially costly for the incumbent party in Congress, because economic growth will be worse.”

Trebbi said, however, that he could see a “silver lining for the Republican Party” emerging if the rate hike helps stabilize price dynamics and “substantially flatten” the Treasury yield curve.

If that happens, he said, “This could be read by voters as a sign of policy competence and enhanced stability, validating the incumbent party.”

Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) chief elections analyst Geoffrey Skelley also expects the immediate economic impact to be minimal, but he said the rate hike will likely “continue to feed into a narrative that inflation is worse than it should be, that the economic status quo is not great.”

“There’s no reason to think that this news is going to somehow produce a wave of economic optimism, which is already a problem for the president’s party,” he added. “And this news isn’t going to help.”

The decision also puts Warsh at odds with President Trump, whobacked him for the position after repeatedly demanding the Fed cut rates.

At a rally in North Carolina on Wednesday night, Trump directed his ire at the Fed’s board of governors, which voted unanimously to raise rates.

“I told Kevin, I said, ‘You might as well vote with the board because it’s just not going to matter.’ The board is very hostile,” he continued. “They’re very political. They’re doing the wrong thing. They’re a bunch of politicians.”

“It’s shame because it’s too high an interest rate,” he added.

▪ The Hill : Warsh says Fed cares ‘very much’ about AI developments.

▪ The Hill : Federal Reserve delivers unwelcome news to Trump.

White House chief of staff Susie Wiles said Wednesday that she is “cancer free” after her pathology results came back clear following an appointment at the Mayo Clinic this week. Wiles was diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer earlier this year.

Independent Rep. Kevin Kiley (Calif.) said he will not caucus with the GOP next year if he wins reelection, months after he left the party out of disgust with the national redistricting battle that’s taken place. Kiley said he only currently caucuses with Republicans to keep his committee assignments , and he’s working to change House rules so independents can also hold them.

OpenAI revealed six new incidents of times when its AI systems hid mistakes, made up data or moved files onto the internet without permission as part of a new framework for reporting “misalignment,” The New York Times reported . The company said the incidents happened over the past six months, mostly when the systems were being developed and tested.

Speaker of the House Mike Johnson (R-La.), flanked by Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.), speaks during a news conference on Capitol Hill, Sept. 15, 2026, in Washington. (Jose Luis Magana, Associated Press)

PARTING SHOTS : The House approved a key bill authorizing additional sanctions on Russia before leaving town a day early Wednesday, starting a weeks-long recess in the lead-up to the November midterm elections.

The chamber passed the legislation by a vote of 262-159, after two Democrats defected to help Republicans pass the rule on Tuesday. The bill now heads to the president’s desk for his signature.

The legislation passed overwhelmingly in the Senate but became controversial in the lower chamber over Democrats’ hesitancy to greenlight additional tariff authority to Trump. Once the bill takes effect, the president will be authorized to implement tariffs on buyers of Russian energy and countries helping Russia evade sanctions.

The bill also extends existing sanctions on Iran.

Before adjourning, the House also almost unanimously passed the bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act, setting it up for consideration in the Senate. The bill would require states to consider establishing standards forcing tech companies to take on more of the electricity costs associated with large AI data centers, though it doesn’t require them to implement regulations.

The House had been scheduled to be in session Thursday for an additional day before the scheduled recess ahead of the midterms, but GOP leaders cut it short . A vote on California environmental rules scheduled for Thursday was moved up to Wednesday.

The move is particularly notable as it will allow lawmakers to head home without having to vote on Rep. Thomas Massie ‘s (R-Ky.) resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth . He had introduced it on Tuesday as a privileged motion, requiring the House to take it up for a vote — or move to “table” the motion — within two legislative days.

That deadline now won’t arrive until the House returns on Nov. 9, after the midterms.

“They’re canceling Congress tomorrow to avoid the vote on IMPEACHING @SecWar,” Massie wrote of the schedule change.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) already canceled two scheduled weeks of the September session planned for the end of the month. He defended the changes Tuesday, noting that much of the House’s legislative work is stalled in the Senate, which will remain in session through the end of September.

▪ The Hill : House races for exit, avoiding Hegseth vote.

▪ The Hill : Massie says he hid Hegseth impeachment from GOP leaders.

▪ The Hill : Senate panel advances farm bill after Mitch McConnell returns.

IN SYNC : Three of Trump’s nominees for health-related positions testified before the Senate health panel for their confirmation hearings on Wednesday, appearing more in line with what lawmakers wanted to hear from them.

The chamber’s Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee heard from Nicole Saphier , Trump’s nominee to be surgeon general; Chris Klomp , the nominee to be deputy health and human services secretary; and Timothy Westlake ; the nominee to be assistant secretary for mental health and substance use.

The hearing was considerably less tense than with some of Trump’s health picks. Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), the panel’s chair, told the nominees he “really enjoyed all of your opening statements.”

Saphier in particular won praise from Cassidy for her remarks that the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is “our greatest tool for combating measles” and is not lethal — breaking with the president .

She also declared her support for a universal birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccine, which both Trump and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have opposed.

The Hill’s Joseph Choi reports the nominees were noticeably less evasive in answering questions than previous Trump nominees. Read more of his takeaways from the hearing for Insider here .

▪ The Washington Post : Cassidy says measles surge will be ‘terrible legacy.’

NEW ADDITION : European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Wednesday that she wants Canada to join the European Union as the bloc’s first associate member as the country is locked in a trade war with the U.S.

The comments from von der Leyen came during her annual State of the Union address. She said she wants to work with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney , who was in attendance, to move forward on her goal.

She said the EU and Canada “see the world” similarly on issues such as artificial intelligence, the climate and defending Ukraine. Carney is set to address the European Parliament on Thursday.

Carney met with von der Leyen and European Parliament President Roberta Metsola and said his country and the European group are “natural partners.”

The trade war between the U.S. and Canada has ramped up in recent weeks, with Trump placing 50 percent tariffs on a wide range of Canadian goods. Canada has responded with 50 percent tariffs of its own on sectors including steel, aluminum and food.

▪ The Associated Press : EU chief proposes social media ban for kids under 13.

▪ Fox News : Five states could be the biggest losers in the Canada trade war.

The president will receive an intelligence briefing at 11 a.m. He will sign executive orders at 5 p.m. and participate in a tele-rally at 6 p.m. He will participate in a Rose Garden dinner at 7 p.m.

The House will convene at 10:30 a.m. for a pro forma session.

Washington Capitals left wing Alex Ovechkin skates in the April 14, 2026, game against the Columbus Blue Jackets in Columbus, Ohio. (Sue Ogrocki, Associated Press)

THIN ICE : NHL superstar Alexander Ovechkin is under fire after he appeared in a campaign ad promoting Russian President Vladimir Putin ‘s political party ahead of the country’s legislative elections this weekend.

The Hill’s Dominick Mastrangelo reports this is just the latest episode in Ovechkin’s long-standing relationship with Putin, who has been widely denounced by the international community over human rights abuses within Russia and most recently for the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

The video showed Ovechkin appearing alongside several other Russian athletes in addition to celebrities and politicians. The ad featured Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov urging viewers to “stand united.”

Ovechkin lives in Russia during the NHL offseason, and his ties to Putin have been well documented throughout the Russian leader’s time in office, Mastrangelo reports.

The ad came out as Ovechkin is about to begin what’s expected to be his final season in the league with the Washington Capitals. Ovechkin has spent his entire career with the Capitals and became the NHL’s all-time leading goal scorer in the 2024-25 season.

The Capitals responded to the criticism in a statement to The Athletic, saying Ovechkin appeared in it only on his own behalf after being asked “by his country” to appear in the ad. The response only added to the backlash.

Rep. Joe Wilson (R-S.C.) urged the NHL to get involved, writing a letter to NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman on Wednesday to ask him to review the situation . Wilson described Ovechkin’s involvement as “incredibly alarming” and called on Bettman to clarify the league’s policy on its players appearing in political ads.

Ovechkin hasn’t directly commented on the ad or the controversy.

▪ Reuters : What to know about Russia’s parliamentary elections.

▪ The Hill Insider : How Russian dissidents are pressing for action on Putin in D.C.

Iowa state Rep. Josh Turek, a Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate, talks to supporters before a neighborhood canvassing event, May 31, 2026, in Waukee, Iowa. (Charlie Neibergall, Associated Press)

EYES ON IOWA : There are increasing signs that Democrats have an opportunity for notable gains in Iowa, a state that they have lost handily to Trump in each of the past three presidential cycles.

Democrats have already been hopeful about their chances of flipping both Iowa’s governor’s mansion and Senate seat this year behind candidates they view as strong contenders. The DDHQ polling average shows Democratic state Auditor Rob Sand leading Republican businessman Zach Lahn by more than 5 points.

The Senate race has been seen as somewhat more of a reach for Democrats, but state Rep. Josh Turek (D) is essentially neck and neck with GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson in the polling average.

A few other indicators have recently suggested Iowa’s more in play. The election handicapper Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifted its rating of the race for the House seat that Hinson is vacating on Wednesday from “Leans Republican” to “Toss-up.”

And some Iowa Republicans have made moves hinting they are feeling the pressure too. GOP Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn both flipped Tuesday night to support a House war powers resolution to restrict Trump’s authority in the Iran war after having opposed previous resolutions.

Both House members are key Democratic targets in November.

Hinson has meanwhile released multiple ads in the past week emphasizing her bipartisanship, saying she is working with both parties to lower the cost of living and expand healthcare for veterans .

▪ The Hill : Ocasio-Cortez sees confidence in her White House chances grow.

▪ The Hill : Kansas’s former GOP governor backs Democrat for Senate.

Move over, evangelicals: Mainline Christians are the 2026 swing voter , Rev. Jennifer Butler writes in The Hill.

Federal judges are being targeted with pizza doxxing; no one has been held to account , Jeremy Fogel and Amrit Singh write in The Hill.

Sunny, President Barack Obama’s dog, takes a walk at the White House, Sept. 9, 2013, in Washington. (Evan Vucci, Associated Press file)

And finally … It’s Thursday, which means it’s time for the weekly news quiz!

Former President Obama revealed Wednesday that he and his family are mourning the loss of their dog , Sunny. The Portuguese water dog was welcomed into the first family in 2013, one of two dogs that the Obamas had during his administration. So, this week’s quiz will look back on the history of presidential pets in the White House.

Be sure to email your responses to jgans@thehill.com — please add “Quiz” to your subject line.

Donald Trump is among the minority of presidents to not have any pets while in office. How many others also didn’t have any? (One president is debatable but choose the closest answer below.)

Which president had the most pets while in office?

One ongoing storyline during Joe Biden’s presidency was instances of his dogs biting Secret Service agents. Which of his dogs was not involved in such an incident?

articles.title: It’s America’s most important holiday. Did you even know?
articles.summary: The most important national holiday in the U.S. doesn’t earn its citizens a day off from work or school. It wasn’t formally created until 2004, when Sen. articles.body:
The most important national holiday in the U.S. doesn’t earn its citizens a day off from work or school.

It wasn’t formally created until 2004 , when Sen. Robert Byrd (D-W.Va.) quietly inserted it into an omnibus spending bill. Most Americans have no idea when it is celebrated or even what it commemorates.

And yet, given the severity of problems plaguing the American body politic today, there is no question that the most important holiday of the year is today, Constitution Day.

I know. Such a sentiment borders on civic heresy. Everyone knows — especially this year — that the Fourth of July is America’s quintessential patriotic celebration. Baseball games and backyard barbecues, small-town parades and flamboyant Americana attire are now synonymous with our most famous national holiday.

But we have confused America’s birthday with its blueprint.

The Fourth of July is important and certainly worthy of the fanfare and flair. It celebrates the most significant political divorce in human history — our emancipation from English monarchical rule. It inspires us to remember the timeless Jeffersonian truths that constitute the essence of the American creed.

In my hometown of Bakersfield, where concerns about air quality and terrified pets do little to dampen enthusiasm for fireworks, Independence Day often resembles trench warfare as bright explosions fill the night sky late into the evening. Americans rightly celebrate liberty with patriotic aplomb.

But Constitution Day deserves equal if not greater attention because of where we find ourselves as a nation circa 2026.

It is not simply that Americans are civically ignorant. They have been for a long time . Surveys documenting our constitutional illiteracy stretch back decades, from academic studies to late night comedy sketches . What’s different today is the nature of our ignorance. Instead of a gaping void of innocent obliviousness, our ignorance pulses with hostility, a new and broadening illiberality pointing towards a future increasingly estranged from our best civic traditions.

Modern Americans have fully embraced the ethos of Independence Day — a spirit of loudly asserting individual rights and demanding ever-expanding freedoms. Constitution Day celebrates something different — more understated but just as monumental: the day thirty-nine delegates signed the document they submitted to the states for ratification. The Constitution was more than a correction to the Articles of Confederation. It was an ambitious attempt to join thirteen semi-independent states into a single republic and create an enduring framework for a new human experiment in democratic self-government.

And this new Constitution did not merely protect liberty. It also made demands of its new citizens. These demands have largely been forgotten in our era. Constitution Day should do more than celebrate, commemorate, and coronate an important document. It should awaken us to the other face of democracy — not of freedom, liberty, and rights, but of duties, obligations and civic responsibility.

The spirit of 1776 celebrates liberty. The spirit of 1787 asks a different question: What kind of citizens must we become if liberty is to long endure?

Freedom can only endure only within constitutional conditions sustained by citizens who understand what it takes to preserve a republic. Former President Barack Obama spoke of these habits in his 2018 eulogy of the late Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) , fondly recalling that McCain would occasionally visit the White House, where the two men would speak frankly about the issues of the day. Despite deep and authentic differences, and despite having run against one another in a presidential campaign, Obama remembered that he and McCain “never doubted we were on the same team. For all of our differences, we shared a fidelity to the ideals for which generations of Americans have marched and fought and sacrificed and given their lives.”

This speech is less than a decade old, and yet the words feel as if they belong in the same era as Daniel Webster’s moving tribute to his rival Henry Clay on his passing in 1852. Listen to Bill Clinton’s soaring tribute to George H.W. Bush on the night of his presidential victory in 1992 or Ronald Reagan’s 1986 remarks at a dinner honoring Tip O’Neill.

In contrast, today we reward performative outrage over any sort of prudent governance or honest conversation. Compromise, coalition-building, and consensus are dismissed as weaknesses rather than recognized as constitutional necessities in a large and diverse republic.

Governing, we once understood, is the ultimate form of adulthood. Now, I fear, we perpetually act as civic children.

Broad swaths of the electorate have little appreciation for the difficult work of constitutional government. Celebrity outshines public service, social media bravado acting as a gratuitous surrogate for experience and statesmanship.

The promise of “We the People” becomes strained when we become manic over the “pluribus” while forever neglecting the “unum.” We increasingly silo our political lives into ideological echo chambers, mistake cynicism for sophistication, and judge the legitimacy of our institutions solely by whether our preferred candidate prevails.

On this Constitution Day, we do not need every American to become a constitutional scholar. We need citizens willing to grow up and relax their stridency, mindful of Lincolnesque charity, and accepting that democracy rarely gives any of us everything we want.

Make better arguments. Work harder to understand our political adversaries. And most of all, remember that democracy is only as vibrant and fair as the convictions of the people entrusted to perpetuate it.

Jeremy S. Adams is the author of “Lessons in Liberty: Thirty Rules for Living from Ten Extraordinary Americans .” He has taught American civics for 28 years in Bakersfield, Calif. and was the 2014 Daughters of the American Revolution California teacher of the year.

James Talarico fuels Democratic hopes of a red-state flip against Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. Talarico says his faith got him into the race and has argued that Christian doctrine affirms his support for progressive policies…
articles.body:
Faith and Christian values have become a focal point of the Texas Senate race as seminarian state Rep. James Talarico fuels Democratic hopes of a red-state flip against Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton .

Talarico says his faith got him into the race and has argued that Christian doctrine affirms his support for progressive policies — while Paxton believes God has “delivered” him through challenges, including an unsuccessful 2023 impeachment , to help keep the Lone Star State in Republican hands.

The dueling messages are on stark display in this year’s midterms, as Republicans across the country sound alarm about what they describe as growing threats to Christian values.

“Christianity is really a part of the political DNA of Texas politics,” said Ross Hunt , a Texas GOP pollster, noting that faith-based appeals are key in the state dominated by Christian “rhetoric and language.”

Talarico and Paxton, who’ve been neck and neck in the toss-up Senate race’s polling, both publicly identify as Christians, but the rivals have approached their faith in different ways on the campaign trail.

In a viral interview released over the weekend, Talarico told Jimmy Kimmel that Jesus would “flip over those fancy desks” if he visited the Senate under current Republican leadership.

“I think he would tell the senators on the floor, ‘Depart from me, for I was hungry and you cut my food assistance. I was sick and you kicked me off Medicaid. I was a stranger and you deported me and my family,’” Talarico said. “And then I think he would flip over those fancy desks on the floor of the U.S. Senate and demand that we take care of all of our neighbors.”

Talarico, a state lawmaker and former public school teacher, is a Presbyterian seminarian who has been studying for a Master of Divinity at Austin Presbyterian Theological Seminary. As one of the Democrats who fled Texas to stall a GOP-led redistricting plan last year, he saw his political star rise with viral remarks in the state legislature and church sermons .

He’s argued that the Bible supports gay marriage, abortion and other progressive policies, drawing the ire of Republicans.

“The challenge here is that James Talarico comes from a segment of Christianity that is small and getting smaller, and that is progressive Protestantism,” said Matthew Wilson, a political science professor at Southern Methodist University in Texas who’s focused on religion and politics.

“His positions are completely indistinguishable from nonreligious Democrats,” he continued. “So I think that’s something that Paxton supporters want to try to call him on.”

Paxton, who defeated Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) in the GOP Senate primary with the help of an endorsement from President Trump, used the GOP midterm convention stage in Dallas last week to blast Talarico over comments that the Democrat has since walked back , including a 2021 remark that “God is nonbinary,” which he said while arguing against Republican legislation on transgender children in youth sports.

Paxton asked the convention crowd for both “your prayers” and “your votes.”

Like Talarico, the Republican Senate nominee is a devout Christian, though a series of controversies has drawn sharp theological rebuke from Democrats.

Paxton went through a high-profile divorce with state Sen. Angela Paxton (R), who filed for the separation on “biblical grounds” amid his campaign last year. And Talarico was one of 121 state lawmakers who voted to impeach Paxton on corruption charges in 2023, before the state attorney general was acquitted by the state Senate.

Paxton leaned into his religious beliefs when discussing his past legal troubles on Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick’s (R) podcast in June .

“I truly believe that God just delivered me, not because I am a great person, because God is sovereign and he does what he wants to do,” Paxton said.

Wilson argued that the Republican nominee has enjoyed traditional support from evangelical Christians, but he noted the top prosecutor “has a hard time leaning explicitly into faith-based themes because of his personal, ethical and marital struggles.”

Hunt, however, cautioned against viewing the religious messaging from the two candidates as “a battle between two extreme versions of Christianity.”

Instead, Hunt says Texas voters view this race “as a contrast between someone who is actually Christian, in the person of Paxton — albeit a flawed individual who will reliably fight for Christian positions — and someone who is sort of pretending to be a Christian.”

Around 67 percent of Texas voters identified as Christians between 2023 and 2024, including 27 percent as evangelical Protestants and 22 percent as Catholics, according to data from the Pew Research Center . Twenty-six percent were not affiliated with a religion, while a small minority of this population was Jewish, Muslim, Buddhist or Hindu.

“What some analysts call the ‘God Gap’ has become huge in American politics,” Wilson said. For decades, “white, churchgoing Christians of all denominational stripes have become more and more Republican.”

“One of the things that initially distinguished Talarico and got a lot of national Democrats excited about him was that he was a Democrat who was not afraid to speak the language of faith. And Democrats feel like they need to reconnect with Christian America, and they think that Talarico might be able to do that,” Wilson said.

Still, a Fox News poll from July showed 78 percent of white evangelicals supported Paxton over Talarico, and 57 percent of “regular worship attendees” backed the attorney general.

In an August Texas Public Opinion Research survey , in which the Democrat posted a 7-point lead against his GOP opponent, Talarico performed better among Catholic and Orthodox Christian voters, while Paxton gained more support from Protestant and evangelical Christians.

Decision Desk HQ’s polling aggregates now show Talarico roughly 4 points ahead of Paxton in the red state, where Democrats haven’t won statewide in decades.

Nancy Zdunkewicz , a Democratic pollster and the founder of Z to A Research, argued Paxton’s past scandals, coupled with an unfavorable national political landscape for Republicans and a competitive Democratic candidate, could create the “perfect storm” to flip this seat.

“There are a lot of Republicans who are just demoralized and don’t want to get out there this year,” she said. “And then, you need a Democrat who’s hard to hang anything damaging on, who’s just like a good, popular Democrat, and we seem to have all of those things.”

Texas Republican consultant Vinny Minchillo argued that although Talarico is “trying to battle Paxton for” the Texas churchgoer demographic, the Democrat faces an uphill climb to reach a bloc that’s long sided with the GOP.

“Paxton typically does very well with churchgoers. That is a strong suit for him,” Minchillo said. He also argued that Talarico’s past comments will dog the Democrat as Texas Christians head to the polls in November.

“From now until election day, there’s no getting around that,” Minchillo said.

What we’ve learned from the 2026 primary cycle:

The 2026 midterm primary season offered curveballs, upsets, candidates leaving the field only to rejoin weeks later, and no shortage of lessons. We chatted with a few experts to get their take on what they took away from this crazy primary cycle.

Primary polling is inherently harder than predicting a general election

Much inked has been spilled this season on the gap between what public polling forecasts has forecasted about competitive races and the actual election turnout.

Some of the most prominent examples included the Michigan Senate Democratic primary and the Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial race. Public polling ahead of the contests suggested that Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong would easily prevail in their primaries.

In the end, El-Sayed, a progressive, narrowly beat centrist Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) while Hong, a democratic socialist, lost to establishment-favorite Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley .

“It probably was a helpful thing to learn or be reminded of that there’s simply a type of election in which uncertainty is much greater than it is in a November election,” Charles Franklin , director of the Marquette Law School Poll, told us.

“The question of whether you need to learn that lesson that there can be late change and therefore wait until the last possible second to do your final poll — that’s much more of a judgment call,” he added, saying he could be open to conducting a later poll closer to the primary in the future.

But that doesn’t mean primary polls are useless, either, Franklin argued.

“It doesn’t mean that you aren’t capturing the strengths of the candidates or the growth of new issues,” he said. “And if you think those things are at all important, then you should still want to do primary polls.”

Polling can influence, rather than inform races

Mark Jones , a political science professor at Rice University, also noted that shady polling has started to serve as a way to influence the narrative of races. That theme became a focal point when pollster Median Strategies shut down its operation after admitting that several of its polls regarding the Wisconsin governor’s primary and Los Angeles mayoral race were fake. The revelations come amid deep distrust around the accuracy of polling.

“You have increasingly campaigns and interest groups driving a lot of these polls. Some openly, but many not openly,” Jones said, “but they all have an agenda, and their agenda is not to inform, not to educate.”

“A lot of these other polls out there — you have to wonder, you know, who’s financing it and what is their ulterior motive?”

The Democratic establishments’ brand is weak

For Kyle Kondik, managing editor of Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia Center for Politics, one of the biggest lessons came from taking the temperature of the Democratic primary electorate.

“There’s just more of an appetite for outsider candidates on the Democratic side than I think there has been in the past,” Kondik said, noting the dynamic of how GOP establishment’s brand has grown weaker over the last 15 years, ultimately becoming replaced by President Trump’s politics.

Democrats’ “establishment is weaker now, too, and so … there’s just kind of more fluidity in the primary electorates of both parties now,” Kondik said.
