As the midterm cycle heats up, we’re asking folks in the elections space what they’re consuming on and off the campaign trail.

Charles Franklin is Marquette University’s professor of law and public policy and also the director of the Marquette Law School p oll in Milwaukee, Wis. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

President Lincoln’s Cooper Union speech from the 1860 campaign.

And in fact, driving back from Milwaukee, I listened to the audible version of his entire hour 15-minute Cooper Union speech about the expansion of slavery into the territories, the positions of the Founding Fathers on the expansion of slavery and federal control over slavery and federal lands. So yes, indeed, I am 170 years out of date on my elections.

I have stopped snacking. That’s the joy of Type 2 diabetes. I drink substantial amounts of water as my snack.

But honest to God, in a past year, I could eat bags of potato chips very happily. I’ve always been “a fat and salt guy” rather than “a sugar guy,” but I have given up all of that. Sad to say.

What album or podcast do you have on repeat?

“Rewind,” which is a weekly political news show produced by Wisconsin Eye — the state version of C-SPAN, and “Wis Politics,” which is a political newsletter in the state.

“The Old-Fashioned Conservatives” is one of the conservative podcasts that I listen to. “Inside Wisconsin Politics,” is the podcast produced by public radio and public television. Also, “The Down Ballot,” which is a national podcast on lower-level races around the country.

And “The Recombobulation Area,” which is a Milwaukee-based website and podcast.

I decaffeinated about five years ago. I still drink two 20-ounce decaf coffees a day for the placebo effect, but I don’t actually drink caffeinated drinks anymore.

What TV show are you watching right now?

“My Brilliant Career” on Netflix. It’s about a young woman in Australia, circa 1900, and it’s sort of a classic English, “Pride and Prejudice” show. A documentary on the city of New York by Rick Burns, Ken Burns’s brother, and Ken Burns’s documentary on The Shakers.

We watch trash, too. We’re certainly watching “Reacher.” I don’t want to make it all sound like it’s PBS all the time. We need our blood and guts too.

What is your favorite place to eat in Wisconsin?

Matsumoto in Sparta, Wis., — a little town between Madison and La Crosse. They have some of the best ramen in the state, and my daughter and I have tried ramen all over the state. We had a previous favorite in Milwaukee called Hungry Sumo, but I’m pleased to say that Matsumoto takes the cake. It is just fantastic.

If you want red meat, then The Tornado Room in Madison is unbeatable, and I also really like Lovechild in Lacrosse. It is really good if you can get in. To my annoyance, they don’t take reservations.

AAPI voters shift toward GOP in Texas, but remain competitive bloc: analysis

Asian American and Pacific Islander (AAPI) Texans have shifted sharply to the right in recent years, according to a new report, but the bloc remains competitive as a high-stakes Senate race shakes the Lone Star State.

A new report from Asian Texans for Justice, a non-partisan non-profit, found that Texas now boasts the third-largest AAPI population among the 50 states, behind California and New York — and the fifth-highest AAPI growth rate of any state, almost triple the growth rate among Texans overall.

Democrats had the upper hand in 2022 and 2024, with roughly 4 in 10 AAPI Texans to Republicans’ 3 in 10. But that’s flipped in the last two years, with the share of AAPI Texas Republicans jumping roughly 11 points and Democrats falling by a similar margin. The share of AAPI Texans who identify as independent has stayed roughly the same in recent years, at roughly 3 in 10.

The growing electorate is competitive for both parties, though. While a 51-percent majority of white Texans identify as Republican and 63 percent of Black Texans identify as Democratic — but no party represents a majority of the state’s AAPI bloc.

In a sign of the bloc’s potential power in a critical Senate race, Democrat candidate James Talarico launched an “AAPI Texans for Talarico” WhatsApp channel aimed at reaching the bloc as the general election nears.

“This campaign is about meeting people where they are — and that includes the hundreds of thousands of AAPI Texans who use WhatsApp to reach their friends and family. The only way to take on this broken, corrupt political system is by uniting all Texans and reaching voters across the state,” Talarico said in a statement from his campaign.

articles.title: Los Angeles news helicopter crash: What we know about victims, investigation
articles.summary: Three people died when a local television news helicopter crashed Tuesday night in Los Angeles’ Chatsworth neighborhood while covering a Metro bus crash that claimed the lives of two bus passengers in the same area.
articles.body:
( KTLA ) — Three people died when a local television news helicopter crashed Tuesday night in Los Angeles’ Chatsworth neighborhood while covering a Metro bus crash that claimed the lives of two bus passengers in the same area.

As the NTSB begins its investigation into the chopper crash, reporter Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw are being mourned by their colleagues at KNBC NBC4 in Los Angeles and across the area’s journalism community.

Here’s what we know about the crash and the three victims who lost their lives.

The news helicopter was providing live aerial coverage of a fatal collision involving an SUV and a Metro bus for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 when it fell from the sky just before 7 p.m., crashing between two commercial buildings at 9151 N. Mason Ave.

The blaring sound of a warning could be heard as the camera angle started to descend.

“You can’t pull up?” Moreno asks Marciniw. The camera starts shaking, and then the signal cuts out.

The explosion caused several nearby vehicles and storage containers to erupt in flames.

“NTSB is investigating the Sept. 15 crash of a Eurocopter AS 350 B2 helicopter in Chatsworth, California,” the agency posted at 2:49 a.m. Wednesday.

The NTSB had not released any preliminary cause of the crash as of Wednesday morning, only telling Nexstar’s KTLA, “We continue to gather information at this time.”

At Wednesday’s press conference, investigator-in-charge Fabian Salazar said that investigators will be on scene “pretty much all day” gathering evidence, including witness statements.

A witness at the scene told KTLA her husband noticed something unusual about the helicopter before it went down.

“I didn’t see it, but my husband did. He did say that it was swaying,” Allyona Sevanesian said. “And then immediately after, it was the cloud of smoke.”

Anyone with information about the crash is asked to come forward by emailing witness@ntsb.gov.

A preliminary report on the crash will be issued within 30 days, Salazar said. A report determining the final cause could take up to 18 months to be released.

In a statement posted on its website, NBC4 and Telemundo 52 said: “We are deeply saddened to share that a helicopter providing aerial news coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 was involved in a fatal accident in Los Angeles on Tuesday evening. We extend our heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives.”

Moreno and Marciniw were both employees of Angel City Air, which also owns and operates KTLA’s Sky5 helicopter.

Both Southern California natives, Moreno and Marciniw began flying together in 2023, NBC Los Angeles said.

Marciniw was a 1974 graduate of Burbank High School, and Moreno graduated from Chapman University in 2010, earning a degree in broadcast journalism and political science, according to NBC4.

The third victim killed Tuesday night was reportedly not on the aircraft but was on the ground in a business parking lot in the area where the chopper crashed. The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner’s Office has identified him as Edy Gutierrez Mejia, 29.

Mayor Karen Bass said during a Tuesday news conference that it was a “very, very, very tragic day in Los Angeles.” She continued, “Our hearts are with those impacted by the bus collision and the helicopter crash, and with the entire community who lost members of their team while they were doing their job.”

News helicopter crashes are rare, but they have happened, and they highlight the dangers of flying.

At least 16 people have died in news helicopter crashes since 2000 in the United States.

In one incident in Seattle in 2014, two journalists for KOMO-TV were killed as the news station’s helicopter crashed just after departing the station’s helipad. The victims were identified as pilot Gary Pfitzner and KOMO photographer Bill Strothman.

In Phoenix in 2007, two helicopters from two different TV stations – KNXV and KTVK – collided in mid-air while covering a police pursuit. The pilots and photographers on both choppers were killed on impact.

The victims on board the KTVK chopper were identified as pilot Scott Bowerbank and photographer Jim Cox. Those on board the KNXV chopper were identified as reporter Craig Smith and photographer Rick Krolak.

“These pilots are incredibly well-trained. They’re experts at what they do. So to have this happen, what I think about is what could have caused this. Obviously they did a pre-flight check. For it to go down so quickly, it’s hard for me to imagine,” said Jennifer York, former KTLA Morning News chopper reporter.

Over her 14-year career, York has covered pursuits, earthquakes, wildfires and other breaking news. But she said safety always came before the rush to get the story.

“This is just absolutely horrific. It’s almost unfathomable because of how well they take care of their chopper,” she said. “Checking everything from the blades to the equipment. I mean, there’s nothing that would ever go untouched. And if there was ever a sense, ever a sense, that something could go wrong, we would not launch. We would absolutely not launch.”

Back in March 2014, KTLA’s Sky5 helicopter made an emergency landing, with smoke pouring from the aircraft.

Clogged oil caused a terrifying scene, but KTLA’s photographer and pilot luckily walked away unharmed.

KTLA’s Tony Kurzweil, Sandra Mitchell and Josh DuBose contributed to this report.

articles.title: Judge Judy retiring from TV because son ‘finally ready’ to take over
articles.summary: The long-running television star is celebrating the 30th anniversary of “Judge Judy.”
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Judge Judy is saying goodbye to her time on TV after three decades.

Judith Sheindlin announced Wednesday on “ Good Morning America ” that she is “retiring from in front of the camera TV bench.”

“Why? Why now?” Co-host Lara Spencer asked Sheindlin.

“A couple of good reasons. First of all, he was ready,” she said, referring to her son, Adam Levy, who has his own TV court show, which is produced by his mother.

“And, you know, I’ve aged pretty well over the years. Reasonably. I look better than my grandmother did at my age, which didn’t take a lot,” Scheindlin continued. “But it’s time for me to— and I’m still going to be creative, still out there.”

She added, I’m just going to take the message and put it in a little bit of a different form. I’m going to become the Benjamin Button of court.”

The long-running television star is celebrating the 30th anniversary of “Judge Judy,” the show that made her a household name. The program, which aired on CBS, ended in 2021 after 25 seasons.

Her current show on Amazon Prime, “Judy Justice,” will end in October, she confirmed to People Magazine .

“I have a lot of other things of interest,” Scheindlin said.

The TV judge is also creating an adult animated series titled “Judyverse.”

“I don’t want to do hair and makeup anymore, but I still want my message to get out there,” she told People. “I don’t have to prove anything else. I did it.”

articles.body:
The U.S. Appeals Court for the 8th Circuit will wade into the Missouri’s congressional map dispute on Thursday.

The hearing in a federal suit filed by Rep. Bob Onder (R-Mo.) follows a week after the U.S. Supreme Court blocked a federal judge’s ruling in another suit that would have allowed a 2025 GOP-favored map to stay in effect. Lawmakers have argued reverting to the 2022 district map this close to elections would cause chaos.

The future of the Kennedy Center hangs in the balance, as the board closed the performing arts venue on Wednesday. Ex-officio board member Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) asked a federal judge to call an emergency hearing for an explanation about the closure.

The Justice Department has been ordered to respond by Thursday morning. Beatty’s legal team wants a “high-level decisionmaker” at the Kennedy Center to be there if a hearing happens.

President Trump is at the White House on Thursday after a Wednesday trip to North Carolina for a rally with Senate candidate Michael Whatley (R). He’ll sign executive orders and host a Rose Garden dinner.

The Senate will take its next vote on the Protect College Sports Act Thursday morning.

Meanwhile, House members headed home Wednesday after Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) ended their session early — putting representatives on a seven-week recess that extends past Election Day in November.

articles.body:
Republican strategist Karl Rove said he is backing a Democrat in a Texas state race after recent controversy surrounding the Republican candidate.

“This November, I’ll vote for only the second Democrat in my life. The first was Lt. Gov. Bob Bullock in 1994, because I thought he would work with Republicans,” Rove wrote in an opinion piece for The Wall Street Journal published Tuesday.

“The second will be Mr. French’s opponent, Jon Rosenthal. The GOP’s stables need a cleaning. This is a good place to start,” he added.

Over the weekend , Texas Republicans condemned the Republican candidate making a bid to be the state’s railroad commissioner, Bo French, due to a post about University of Texas at Austin students of South Asian descent.

French’s post featured South Asian students at a Texas football game, with the candidate suggesting people of South Asian heritage were taking over the school’s population.

The Republican originally shared a screenshot of a post on the social platform X that showed the students alongside a caption reading “Bollywood University.” French later showed a similar image with a caption reading: “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.”

“The GOP has a growing number of Bo Frenches—and not only in Texas. Conservatism and the party it dominates have an increasing number of bigoted advocates of a ‘heritage America,’ composed of white descendants of the original European settlers,” Rove wrote in his Journal piece.

The Hill has reached out to French’s campaign for comment.
